#9034. Here’s What to Know About the Nike Vaporfly 5

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nike announced a whole slate of innovations it has in the works, including a new method for creating Air units, the return of the Nike Free, and a look at the future of its sportswear. But the most interesting product unveiling is the Vaporfly 5—Nike is calling it the “most aggressive Vaporfly yet.”

The big highlight is that the road racing shoe is basically going to have a “spring” in it. “At the center of Vaporfly 5 is a new, wave-shaped Flyplate,” Nike’s announcement read. “A ripple through the midfoot creates a spring-like sensation under the arch.”

I got a look at the prototype in Chicago last month, when I visited Nike’s headquarters during marathon weekend. There, I asked Bret Schoolmeester, vice president of running footwear product, if he was concerned about calling the shoe a spring. He is not, and told me that shoes basically serve as springs already given the bouncy modern foams being used.

Remember back to the first carbon-plated shoes, when much of the uproar around them was because people believed the plates would act like springs. That’s not really what came to fruition, as we found that the plates basically were used as stiffening mechanisms to create leverage.

World Athletics rules permit a plate in a single layer, and that’s what Nike is technically creating here. The difference is in the shaping. The bump in this new plate, combined with the midsole geometry, will allow the plate to flex when you land and snap back to shape to propel you ahead.

Nike also looked at ways to strip weight, which you can see through the big carve-outs in the foam, the super thin Vapor Mesh upper, and sparse use of Goatek outsole. Another weight-saving measure is adding ZoomX LT, the lightweight version of ZoomX that we saw in the Alphafly 4. A thin layer of that sits between the plate and your foot, while the standard ZoomX is used between the plate and the road for control and responsiveness.

With these changes, Nike is positioning this shoe to be a shorter-distance road racing shoe. Given the overhaul of the Alphafly 4 and the announcement of the Apex, a hyper shoe designed for elite marathoners, the Vaporfly is being pitched for races up to 13.1 miles. Sure, some runners will lace it up for a full marathon, though it’s going to be lighter and snappier to excel at faster speeds.

The shoe won’t be available until “fall 2027,” but Nike is showing it off early as it drums up excitement for upcoming footwear and apparel at its World of Athletes event.

Beyond the Vaporfly 5, there were some other cool new innovations announced, including “Tuned Air.” Through a new manufacturing process, Nike is able to create lighter Air units more quickly, which can be customized for various applications.

I spoke with Phil McCartney, executive vice president, chief innovation, design and product officer, last week about Tuned Air. He explained that through a proprietary digital print and selective lamination process, Air units can be created with different amounts of cushioning and support. Those characteristics are delivered not only through the physical geometries of the Air unit, but also by varying the pressure within each unit.

Nike has previously talked about “Tuned Air,” and we saw it in use with the Pegasus Plus 2. But that was really just offering a few different air bags. The idea is that bigger shoes are worn by bigger runners and, thus, bigger Air units with greater gas pressures are required. So, shoes any smaller than a women’s 7.5 (M6) got an Air unit that’s 9.5 mm thick with 15 psi. Moving on up to a men’s 10.5 (W12), the bag gains 2 mm thickness. And, those runners with larger feet sit atop the 11.5mm-thick unit pumped up with 20 psi.

These new units, however, are different altogether. Nike found a way to remove the need for pins and rigid zones that formed the Air units, so that each can offer better cushioning and responsiveness.

Like the Vaporfly 5, Tuned Air won’t make an appearance until later in 2027. The prototype shoe teased in the image above has one massive Air unit making up the entire midsole. No word yet on which model or franchise that shoe will reside.

While we wait, the fastest Nike available to any of us remains the Alphafly 4.

Jeff is Runner-in-Chief for Runner’s World and the director of product testing. He has tested and reviewed running shoes, GPS watches, headphones, apparel, and more for nearly two decades. He regularly tests more than 100 pairs of shoes each year, and once had a 257-day streak running in different models. Jeff can usually be found on the roads, racing anything from the mile to a marathon, but he also enjoys racing up mountains and on snowshoes. When he’s not running, you’ll probably find him hanging from a ladder making repairs and renovations to his house (he’s also director of product testing for Popular Mechanics).

Picture this: you settle into a fully flat bed at 35,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, the city lights of New York fading behind you. In seven hours, you'll be in Paris. But right now, in this seat — a seat that costs upward of $6,000 in cash — you paid 53,000 points to be here. That's the Air France Business Class experience on the JFK–CDG route, and it's one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions available to the ChooseFI community today. Let's talk about the math, because the math is what makes this a genuine FI moment. A round-trip business class ticket between New York and Paris on Air France routinely retails for $3,000 on the low end and climbs to $6,000 or beyond during peak travel periods. At 53,000 Flying Blue miles one-way, you're looking at a value of **5.7 to 11.3 cents per point** — in a world where most points are considered excellent at 1.5 to 2 cents. You are, quite literally, squeezing 3 to 7 times the average value out of every mile you've earned. The pricing inefficiency here is real and it's structural. Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program releases discounted award seats monthly, sometimes cutting standard pricing by 25–50%. When a Promo Reward surfaces on a transatlantic business class route, the gap between what you'd pay in cash and what you pay in miles becomes almost absurd. A $4,000 cash ticket redeemable for 53,000 points you transferred at no cost from your Chase Sapphire Reserve? That's **7.5 cents per point** — money that your future self will thank you for. Beyond the numbers is the *experience* itself. Air France's long-haul business class product on the Boeing 777-300ER features a fully flat bed in a 1-2-1 configuration, direct aisle access from every seat, genuine French hospitality, and a meal service that feels like a restaurant, not an afterthought. This isn't a product you suffer through — it's one you savor. For a community that builds wealth intentionally so they can live fully, this is exactly what travel rewards are designed to unlock: a world-class experience at a fraction of the cost, because you understood the system.

Monthly promotional pricing makes premium European travel consistently accessible

The core mechanism here is Flying Blue's Promo Rewards program, and once you understand how it works, you'll never look at transatlantic business class the same way again.

Flying Blue is Air France-KLM's frequent flyer program and a member of the SkyTeam alliance. Unlike many loyalty programs that use a static award chart, Flying Blue uses dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate based on demand, route, and season. That sounds like a disadvantage, and for standard awards it often is. But Flying Blue offsets this with a monthly release of Promo Rewards: a curated list of routes where award seats are released at 25–50% below standard dynamic pricing, often with surcharges waived entirely.

This is the inefficiency. When Air France wants to stimulate demand on a specific route in a given month, it uses Promo Rewards to attract award bookings. The airline gets seats filled; you get business class to Paris for 53,000 miles instead of potentially 80,000+ at standard dynamic rates. It's a win-win — if you know to look for it.

The transfer ecosystem is what makes this accessible. Flying Blue partners with every major transferable points currency at a 1:1 ratio:

The practical implication: if you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, Amex Platinum, Amex Gold, Citi Strata Premier, Capital One Venture X, or Bilt Mastercard, you already have a direct pipeline to Flying Blue miles. Most transfers are instant, meaning you can spot a Promo Reward, confirm the seat exists, transfer points, and book — all in the same afternoon. That speed matters because Promo Reward seats can disappear quickly.

One nuance worth naming: fuel surcharges. On standard Flying Blue awards for Air France and KLM-operated flights, the program passes through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $200–$500 to your redemption. However — and this is critical — Promo Reward bookings typically eliminate these surcharges, meaning you pay the miles cost plus only government taxes. Always confirm surcharge status before booking a non-Promo award.

Finally, understand the routing rules: Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into Paris and home from Amsterdam (or vice versa), effectively building a multi-city European trip with a single award booking. The booking window opens 359 days in advance — plan accordingly.

Head to FlyingBlue.com at the beginning of each month — Promo Rewards are typically released in the first week. Navigate to the "Promo Rewards" section under the Awards tab. You're looking for transatlantic routes in business class (referred to as "Business" or "La Première" on the site). Bookmark the page and set a calendar reminder. You can also follow ChooseFI community forums, frequent flyer blogs, and Flying Blue's social accounts, which announce Promo Rewards as they drop. When a JFK–CDG or similar North America–Europe business class Promo Reward appears at 53,000 miles, you're in the window.

Once you've identified a Promo Reward route, search for availability directly on FlyingBlue.com. Use the award search tool, select "Business" class, and enter your travel dates. Promo Reward seats are labeled distinctly in the results. If you see them, note the exact flight numbers, dates, and total miles required before doing anything else. Don't transfer points yet — just confirm the seats exist and are bookable.

Determine which transferable currency you'll use. If you have Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, those are your fastest options — transfers to Flying Blue are instant. Log into your credit card portal (chase.com/ultimaterewards or americanexpress.com/rewards) and confirm you have at least 53,000 points available per person traveling in business class.

Initiate the transfer from your credit card rewards portal. Enter your Flying Blue membership number exactly as it appears on your account. For Chase and Amex, transfers post instantly — refresh your Flying Blue account and the miles should appear within minutes. For Capital One or Bilt, allow 1–2 days. For Marriott Bonvoy, note the 3:1 ratio (you'll need 159,000 Bonvoy points for 53,000 Flying Blue miles) and allow 1–5 days.

Return to FlyingBlue.com, log in with your miles now posted, and complete the award booking. Select the Promo Reward fare, confirm the passenger details, and review the fee breakdown carefully — verify that surcharges are eliminated or minimal. Pay the government taxes (typically $50–$150 transatlantic) with a credit card.

If Promo Reward seats aren't available on your dates, don't give up. Check standard award availability on Flying Blue — the pricing will be higher, but the experience is identical. Alternatively, set up alerts through third-party tools and revisit the search as your travel dates approach. Availability often opens closer to departure as airlines release unsold inventory.

Unlike most airline award programs that set a fixed or dynamic price and leave it, Flying Blue runs a monthly promotional cycle. At the beginning of each month, they release a list of routes with discounted award pricing. These Promo Rewards typically offer 25-40% off the standard mileage price and apply to both economy and business class. The discounted routes change every month, covering different destinations on a rotating basis. This means a route that is not on promotion this month may appear next month. The system rewards patience and monitoring: travelers who check the Promo Rewards page monthly and maintain transfer-ready points in Chase, Amex, or other programs can consistently find premium cabin deals to European destinations.

Let's walk through a real-world example that illustrates exactly why the ChooseFI community gets excited about this redemption.

The Booking: You're flying JFK → CDG in Air France Business Class on a Boeing 777-300ER. It's a Tuesday evening departure — one of the best days for award availability — and you've snagged a Promo Reward seat at 53,000 Flying Blue miles plus approximately $65 in government taxes.

The Cash Alternative: A quick search on Google Flights shows the same seat retailing for $4,200 on that date. That's not an anomaly — transatlantic business class averages $3,000–$6,000 depending on season and advance purchase. At $4,200 in cash versus 53,000 miles, you're extracting 7.9 cents per point in value. Your Chase Ultimate Rewards points just became extraordinarily potent.

The Experience: You arrive at JFK and head to the Air France lounge before departure — accessible as a business class passenger. From the moment you board, the difference from economy is visceral. Your seat in the 1-2-1 configuration means no climbing over a stranger; you have direct aisle access. The seat fully reclines into a 180-degree flat bed with a thick mattress pad and proper bedding — not a glorified recliner, an actual bed. The meal service begins shortly after departure: a starter, a main course with real silverware, a cheese course, dessert, and a selection of French wines that would be at home in a Parisian bistro.

Seven hours later, you land at CDG having slept properly, eaten well, and arrived ready to explore Paris instead of recovering from an overnight in a middle seat. You step off the plane into Terminal 2E, collect your bags, and you're in the city within an hour.

The FI Math: Those 53,000 points came from everyday spending on your Chase Sapphire Reserve — grocery runs, gas, a few restaurant meals over the course of six months. You didn't buy the points. You earned them on purchases you were already making, transferred them in minutes, and unlocked a $4,200 experience for $65 out of pocket. That's the ChooseFI travel rewards system working exactly as designed.

Do this: Set a recurring monthly calendar reminder for Promo Rewards. Promo Rewards drop in the first week of each month and popular routes sell out fast. The readers who consistently land these redemptions aren't lucky — they're systematic. Mark the first Monday of every month as your "check Flying Blue" day.

Do this: Use an open-jaw routing to maximize your Europe trip. Flying Blue allows open-jaw itineraries, meaning you can fly into one city and out of another within a single award booking. Fly JFK → CDG, travel through France, and fly home from AMS → JFK. You've just built a multi-city trip without paying for positioning flights — and used a single 53,000-mile award to do it.

Do this: Transfer points only after confirming availability. This cannot be overstated. Transfers from Chase and Amex are instant, but they are also irreversible. Never initiate a transfer until you have confirmed, with your own eyes, that the award seat is available and bookable. The five-minute shortcut of transferring first has stranded miles in countless accounts.

Avoid this: Booking standard dynamic awards without checking Promo Rewards first. Flying Blue's dynamic pricing on standard awards can be significantly higher than Promo Reward pricing — sometimes 30–50% more miles for the exact same seat. Always check if the month's Promo Rewards include your route before defaulting to a standard award.

Avoid this: Ignoring the surcharge line item. On standard (non-Promo) Flying Blue awards for Air France flights, carrier surcharges can add $200–$500 to your out-of-pocket cost. This doesn't eliminate the value, but it changes the math. Always review the full fee breakdown before confirming. Promo Rewards typically waive these surcharges — another reason to prioritize them.

Do this: Stack earning across multiple cards. You don't need to earn 53,000 points on a single card. Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to Flying Blue at 1:1. Accumulate across programs, then choose the best transfer source when a Promo Reward surfaces. This flexibility is a structural advantage of the ChooseFI approach to travel rewards.

Know your expiry window. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one transaction (even a small earning or redemption) every two years to protect your balance.

This redemption is built for the intentional traveler — someone who has spent time accumulating points on one or more major transferable currencies and is ready to deploy them strategically rather than cash them in for coffee and Amazon gift cards.

Minimum requirements: You'll want at least 53,000 points in a single transferable currency (Chase, Amex, Citi, Capital One, or Bilt) or the ability to combine balances to reach that threshold. No Flying Blue status is required — this is available to any member.

This redemption is rated **moderate**, and that's an honest assessment. The experience itself — transferring points, booking on FlyingBlue.com — is straightforward. What adds complexity is the timing and strategy layer. **What makes it moderately challenging:** 1. **Promo Rewards require patience and timing.** The best pricing surfaces once a month, for specific routes, in limited quantities. You can't always book exactly when you want to travel. The challenge: knowing which account holds what, and when to move miles. **Three tips to make this easier:** - **Use the 359-day booking window.** Flying Blue opens awards 359 days in advance. Get comfortable with the interface before you're racing to book a Promo Reward seat. If you can earn miles and check a website once a month, you can execute this redemption. Thousands of travelers in the ChooseFI community have done it — you're next.

Major US-to-Europe routes like JFK-CDG or JFK-AMS tend to appear on the Promo Rewards list every 2-4 months. Less popular routes may appear less frequently. The key is consistent monthly monitoring so you catch the promotion when it appears for your target destination.

Flying Blue does not offer formal stopover benefits on award tickets. However, you can book a one-way promo award to your gateway city and then add a separate low-cost carrier or train connection to your final destination. Many travelers use this strategy to explore Paris or Amsterdam for a few days before continuing onward.

Yes. Flying Blue miles expire after 24 months of account inactivity. Any qualifying activity resets the clock, including earning miles through a flight, credit card transaction, or transfer partner. A single small transfer from Chase or Amex every two years is sufficient to keep your miles alive.

Both airlines offer lie-flat business class seats with direct aisle access on long-haul aircraft. When booking through Flying Blue, you can choose either airline based on routing, schedule, or cabin preference.

Flying Blue Promo Rewards turn business class to Europe from a special-occasion splurge into a repeatable system. By monitoring monthly promotions, maintaining transfer-ready points across multiple programs, and booking when your route appears at a discount, you can consistently fly lie-flat to European destinations for 50,000-62,000 miles. The fuel surcharges are a real cost to factor in, but even with that overhead, promo business class awards deliver 5-12 cents per mile in value. Set the monthly reminder and let the system work.

#9032. You Don’t Need a Weight Room to Build Cycling Power—You Just Need This One Compact Piece of Equipment

Build core strength, stability, and mobility at home with one compact training tool.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

If a cyclist is able to work strength training into their fitness routine, especially throughout the off-season, then the ceiling for potential power and speed goes up. The challenge is, as cyclists we just want to ride our bikes—driving to a gym, spending an hour or more in the weight room, then driving home is that much less time we’ll get in the saddle.

I’ve spent close to the last decade as a personal trainer, and there is one piece of equipment I have come to prioritize in my home gym—no matter the season. The TRX Suspension Strap System is a versatile, compact, and burlier-than-expected piece of gym equipment. I’ve had the same pair since I was certified almost 10 years ago and they are still in great shape—even after loads of personal use as well as using them for in-home training sessions with clients.

One of the major reasons I continue to use the TRX system in my own workouts is because I can do a full-body strength workout, in a fraction of the time it takes me in the weight room, and I can do it all with one piece of equipment at home. All the TRX system needs is a way to mount it and enough room to do the exercises on the list.

Here, we’ll dig deeper into what TRX Suspension Straps are, why I recommend them to cyclists specifically, and give you a workout to jumpstart your season.

TRX Suspension Straps are a suspension-based training tool designed to be used for bodyweight exercises. They were initially created by Randy Hetrick, a former U.S. Navy SEAL. He wanted to create a piece of fitness equipment that could offer full-body training and fit into a backpack—several iterations later, TRX was born. TRX Suspension Straps are basically a set of adjustable nylon straps that have handles to grab and cradles for feet. Most of the exercises you start with will have both hands on the handles, but as you progress you will start to add exercises with your feet in the cradles instead. The unique thing about this piece of equipment is that it can equally push a high-level athlete as well as offer things like balance improvement exercises. TRX bands can take simple exercises like a plank or a squat and offer modifications to make the exercise easier or create challenging progressions to make the exercise (much) harder. That makes them valuable for cyclists just starting out on a strength-training program or for those of us who have been doing it for years. The other great thing is they pack down really well. I have personally put them in the bottom of a carry-on bag on many trips over the years. You can set them up on everything from a traditional wall anchor to tree limbs and doorjambs. During my in-home personal training days, I had even set them up poolside for a great outdoor session with a client.

Cyclists benefit from some level of strength training off the bike. It’s one of the best ways to build speed, power, and durability. (Our Strength Training for Cyclists program, which is free to members, is packed with training plans, strategies, and expert advice, making it a great place to get started or to elevate your current workouts.) With the TRX system, you can get all the benefits of strength training in with a tool that’s super effective. I like it because you can use it for moves that work your whole body, like an atomic push-up, which is when you perform a pushup with your feet in the bands, or something that isolates a muscle group, like a calf raise. Building a strong and sound core is a key to developing stability through the body.

One great thing about the TRX straps is that almost every exercise you do will help improve core stability. Increasing that stability will allow for better energy transfer through your body as you ride. The straps also are incredible for mobility and stretching, allowing you to get deeper into and out of stretches. They do this by allowing you an extra point of stability when your hands are holding the handles or cradles at the end of the straps.

If you are setting these up in your home gym, you will need a way to mount the straps. They come with a carabiner attached to the straps, but that has to get clipped to something. I typically use a double-length nylon sling used for climbing because I had a few of these lying around that I retired from my climbing rack. TRX also makes specific straps, wall anchors, and even doorjamb anchors to set the straps up on just about anything you can think of. Pro tip—make sure the anchor you use for the straps is strong enough to hold more than bodyweight.

I have been using my own set of the TRX Straps for over a decade now and they show few signs of wear. During my time as a personal trainer, I used the suspension straps for everyone from elite athletes to people in their seventies and eighties just looking to improve balance and mobility. They can handle everything from explosive training days to core and stability training. For cyclists that are looking to build a stronger core, here are a few of my favorite exercises.

You can find our complete expert-recommended workout here. The exercises, demonstrated by Susane Pata, TRX senior master instructor, will build the strength, stability, and mobility cyclists need. You can do the warmup moves anytime you want to wake up your muscles before a ride, and the stretches to loosen up when you’re done.

#9031. 8 Sugar-Free Electrolyte Powders That Don’t Suck

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Skratch Labs Unsweetened Hydration Sport Drink Mix

When it comes to staying hydrated during a workout or race, many athletes opt for sport drinks, and for good reason – these optimized blends contain calories, carbohydrates, and electrolytes in an easily digestible liquid. But these drinks also contain a lot of sugar, and though that’s exactly what your body needs during a workout, that’s not the case for the hours of your day not occupied by swim-bike-run.

But the effects of those workouts linger, especially during the summer months, during peak training periods, or even when we’re ill. The more we sweat, the more water and electrolytes we lose, and we can feel it in a lot of ways: brain fog, headache, muscle cramps, and fatigue.

Water, along with electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium, is quite easy to replenish through whole-food sources, but to fill the gaps (or to rehydrate quickly), many endurance athletes also turn to sugar-free electrolyte drinks, which deliver all of the rehydration without the added sugar. These beverages provide a tasty alternative to drinking plain water all day, which may lead to increased consumption.

To be clear, sugar-free electrolyte drinks shouldn’t automatically be touted as a “healthier” option than traditional sports drinks. They often contain artificial sweeteners, which some studies suggest can negatively impact gut health and potentially lead to other health issues (for more on this, read sports dietitian Matthew Kadey’s deep dive on sugar-free formulations). Many also list “natural flavors” in their ingredient list, which could be just about anything: LMNT, an electrolyte drink that markets itself as having “no sugar” and “no dodgy ingredients,” has recently come under fire for hiding maltodextrin, a sugar with a high glycemic index, as a “natural flavor.”

But sugar-free electrolytes aren’t going anywhere anytime soon; in fact, many popular sports drink manufacturers, including Gatorade, now offer low- and no-sugar versions of their flagship beverages to avoid penalties in countries with sugar taxes and to meet growing consumer demand for sugar-free options.

Whether you’re looking for an electrolyte complement to your high-carb fueling strategy on race day or a hydration boost at the office after a sweaty lunchtime run, sugar-free electrolyte drinks may have a place in your daily nutrition plan. Triathlete editors shook up eight no-sugar electrolyte blends in search of the best – here are their picks.

You might pucker slightly while drinking this sugar-free electrolyte mix. With no sweeteners and real lemon and lime juice in the ingredients, it’s a delightfully tangy way to get in some electrolytes when you don’t need a hefty dose of carbs during or after exercise.

The salted margarita flavor is certainly reminiscent of its namesake, so sip it on the patio as a little end-of-the-day treat to yourself in the summer, or heat up your water before adding it for a great way to warm up in the winter. While you can get these as individual serving packs for about $1 each, the resealable bag offers a slightly more eco-friendly option that saves you 10 cents per serving.

If you detest the taste of stevia but want a palatable everyday electrolyte that supports super light training or days off, Quince offers an affordable option at 67 cents per serving.

With no sweeteners, this mix mostly delivers a salty flavor with a little fruity flair. The citrus flavor is crisp while the watermelon gives off summer vibes, even if you’re using it to recover from a long day of skiing or ice skating with the fam in the winter. But the raspberry was our favorite as the most balanced flavor in the mix. The multi-pack is great if you plan to drink it frequently and don’t want to get burnt out on any one flavor.

If you like lemon-lime Gatorade, you’ll love this formulation from LMNT. The flavor is oddly reminiscent of the neon-green drink served at the soccer games and track meets of your youth, but without the eyebrow-raising ingredients. (As mentioned above, however, LMNT is currently facing accusations of using maltodextrin as a “natural flavor,” which may negate the halo effect for some customers.)

With 1,000mg of sodium, this is a super-salty blend that takes some getting used to at first; we recommend diluting it in more water or trying only half a packet until your taste buds adjust. But after a long ride in the summer sun, the salt and citrus combo hit the spot much like a margarita at your favorite Mexican joint for post-ride burritos.

Instead of loading up on sodium, Just Ingredients follows a 3:1 ratio of potassium to sodium, along with multiple other electrolytes like calcium, magnesium, and chloride. All of this is derived from real-fruit sources: the first three ingredients listed on the package are guava, peach, and mango. This makes for a pleasant flavor, though the formulation is very clumpy, no matter what method is used to shake or stir the powder into water. Try blending into a smoothie for a cool, tropical treat instead.

Cure’s Hydrating Electrolyte Mixes follow the World Health Organization’s Oral Rehydration Solution formula recommendations for the ideal ratio of water, glucose, sodium and potassium to facilitate rapid rehydration.

Despite the presence of stevia and monk fruit as sweeteners, no chemical taste is present, and the watermelon flavor actually tastes like watermelon, not an artificial dupe of it. For best results, shake vigorously and serve ice-cold (paper umbrella optional).

Led by top triathlon coach Natasha Van Der Merwe, Raw Nutrition’s endurance line has gained a steady following with athletes looking for a comprehensive approach to nutrition and fueling. They’ll find it in this formulation, which contains not only the essential electrolytes but also vitamins C, B6, B12, and taurine.

The mix dissolves well and goes down smooth – best of all, the fruit punch flavor is reminiscent of Hawaiian Punch, making it a nostalgic delight to drink both in and out of workouts.

Made with five real fruits (raspberry, coconut, lemon, lime, banana), a sprinkling of beet powder for nitrates, and a blend of unique ingredients not typically seen in electrolyte powders (bamboo silica, anyone?), DryWater claims to give athletes “complete cellular hydration.” Indeed, many of the ingredients are backed by scientific research. However, some feel a bit of a stretch – the sweetener derived from katamfe fruit extract, for example, provides natural sweetness without spiking blood sugar. However, there is limited evidence of DryWater’s claims that the ingredient “supports balanced energy levels [and] promotes better digestion.”

The flavor is strong and lingers, leaving a film on the tongue and inside the mouth. To avoid this effect, consider using only half a packet or diluting the mix with more water.

As a trusted supplement manufacturer, Thorne is a go-to for many athletes looking for tested and certified products by NSF, or the National Sanitation Foundation, which conducts independent testing to ensure ingredient lists are accurate and free of ingredients banned by the World Anti-Doping Agency. That peace of mind pairs well with Thorne’s blood orange flavor – the mix hits the salty-sweet balance perfectly, with a flavor profile that never gets old. Add to your water bottle at work or while running errands to top off electrolytes throughout the day.

#9029. 10-Minute Slow Yoga Practice to Counter the Chaos

Yoga isn’t the answer to everything. But when life gets stressful, your mat is a safe place to land. Amid moments of stress and chaos, a gentle yoga flow made up of intentional movement can help still your racing mind, regulate your breathing, and encourage overall well-being. This practice blends elements of yin yoga and a generally pared-down approach that feels like a truly restful beat rather than another item on your to-do list.

The challenge here, especially when your default state has been “go go go,” is to slow down. It’s almost like you’re retraining your body, and reminding yourself that it’s okay to do so.

Your goal today is relaxation, so you might want to keep a supportive prop—such as like a bolster, pillow, or yoga block—close by.

Begin in Rock Pose today, which is a variation of Child’s Pose. Sit back on your heels, with your toes untucked, and keep your legs close together. Hinge forward to round your upper body over your legs, placing your forehead on your mat or a block. Drape your arms by your sides, palms facing upward, so you create a rock-like shape.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Extend your arms forward and press up onto your hands and knees. With your next inhalation, lower your belly, lift your chin and chest, and arch your back in Cow Pose.

Exhale as you round your back and tuck your chin in Cat Pose.

Repeat Cat and Cow 3 times each, moving with the pace of your breath.

Lower yourself all the way down onto the front side of your body. Widen your feet toward the back corners of your mat. Your elbows will be just underneath your shoulders—or slightly forward if you’re dealing with lower back tension. Then lift your chest and press your palms and forearms into the mat in Sphinx Pose.

If you have a block, you can use it on its highest setting by angling it toward you and allowing your forehead to rest against the support.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Still lying down, stack your hands, elbows bent and pointing toward the edges of mat, and rest your forehead on the backs of your hands.

Start to slide your right knee out to the right side of the mat so it’s about in line with your hip in Half Frog. You want your right leg to have about a 90-degree angle so the inner thigh and calf are facing the floor. Keep resting your forehead on your hands or turn your head to one side.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

When you’re ready, repeat on the opposite side.

From Half Frog Pose with your left knee bent, take a deep breath in. As you exhale, let your left leg extend long and straight behind you. Drape your arms by your sides, palms facing up. Turn your head and your gaze in either direction and let your shoulders round toward the ground. Simply be.

Stay here in a reverse variation of Savasana for 3-5 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Save on editor-tested e-bikes for commuting, cargo hauling, trail riding, and more.

Fall riding season is winding down, but Black Friday is right around the corner. Several e-bike companies and retailers have already rolled out great deals and special promotions on some of our favorite and best-tested electric bikes. There isn’t a single type of electric bike or e-bike rider. These zippy, pedal-assist bikes are perfect for enjoying your local bike paths, riding rail trails with your family, or tackling singletrack adventures. E-bikes are also great for your daily commute, basic transportation, and running errands.

With big savings from brands, now is a great time to score a deal to get some rides in before the snow starts falling!

No matter your budget or riding needs—from commuters to mountain bikers, experienced cyclists and brand-new riders—there is an e-bike for everyone and every age. Our test team rides dozens of electric bikes each year, and these are some of our favorites and the best deals out there right now.

A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

Compared with earlier Aventure versions, the third-generation model rides smoother and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s new torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found previous models had too much torque, but Aventure fixed that issue. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

The Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-road, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths. However, the bike is burly; its weight and components limit its fun on technical singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Aventon also offers a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same big, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price.

Aventon’s Pace 5 REC is a zippy e-bike that’s perfect for weekend cruises around town, the bike path, or even occasional commutes. The brand refined the Pace with a slew of updates, making it one of the best bang-for-your-buck step-throughs on the market. These include connected features (such as GPS tracking and theft deterrence), a powerful 750 Watt motor, regenerative braking, and an impressive 75-mile range. It’s offered in five colors (grey, mint, pink, orange, and teal) and two frame sizes.

The Pace 5 does not come with a rack, fenders, or a suspension fork. If you commute by bike frequently or use your e-bike for running errands, consider paying $200 more for the Level 4.

The Cityscape stands out for its combination of low price, practical features (like a rack and fenders), and a UL-certified battery. Unlike some Amazon brands, Heybike offers a U.S. support line for warranty service or product questions.

Includes FREE accessories: Fast Charger, Running Boards, Frame Bag, Cushions, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Seat, and Orbitor.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Discounted to $1,699, the dual-battery model has up to 120 miles of range and a 28 mph top speed. A single-battery version is also available for $1,399; it boasts an impressive 60-mile range. Need even more battery power? The $1,999 Long Range model goes up to 170 miles from a single charge.

These prices make the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes on the market. And they’re a solid option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike. “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, said Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers and the Essentials package, I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Water-Resistant Panniers, Lock, Elite Headlight, Seatpost, Comfort Saddle, Phone Mount, and Mirrors.

To increase the XP4’s function and fun, the 750 has a 1310-watt peak motor output (200 watts more than the standard model) and an 85-mile range.

Whether you’re riding city streets on your commute or out for a weekend ride, this bike is fast, easy to ride, and a blast to pedal.

Includes FREE accessories: Rear Rack, Fenders, Headlight, and Seatpost.

The XP Lite 2.0 scales back the XP4 750’s top speed and power, with pedal assist topping out at 20 mph, a peak motor output of 819 watts, and a reduced payload capacity of 275 pounds. It also drops the suspension fork found on the XP4, but still delivers an impressive range of up to 80 miles.

However, the XP Lite isn’t simply a stripped-down version of the XP4; it has some major advantages. At 49 pounds (without accessories and options), it’s 26 pounds lighter than the higher-powered model. This makes the Lite much easier to lift and transport. Plus, instead of an 8-speed drivetrain, the XP Lite features a low-maintenance Gates belt drive. That means no greasy chain, no finicky gear adjustments, and a quieter, cleaner ride. Yes, it’s a singlespeed, but the pedal-assist motor easily compensates for all but the steepest hills or heaviest loads.

Includes FREE accessories: Support Seat, Elite Headlight, Suspension Seatpost, and Cargo Package.

Electric trikes are a great choice for many riders, including seniors, people with mobility limitations, and those who need to carry heavy payloads. At $1,699, the Lectric XP Trike2 is an easy-to-ride, stable three-wheeler.

A 750-watt motor with 1,310 peak watts powers the XP Trike up to 17 mph and up to 70 miles of range on a charge. The Trike features a wide, soft seat with back support. Plus, it has a suspension seatpost and suspension fork for added comfort.

With a top speed of 28 mph, 81 miles of range, a 100mm-travel suspension fork, 27.5”x2.6”, a rack, and fenders, the Adventure Neo Allroad Speed’s name fits it to a T. This bike is built for adventures large and small, from commutes to work in the snow or rain, to gravel trails at your local park.

To power the Adventure, Cannondale uses a Bafang 750W rear hub motor and an easy-access 750 Wh removable battery. With its power and wide-range 8-speed drivetrain, you will get up every hill, while Tektro hydraulic disc brakes will control your speed on descents. Plus, it’s available in flashy red or more subdued matte black.

Many “step-through” e-bikes lack a truly low-step design, making them difficult for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, from REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. This makes the CTY a great choice for older riders, those with mobility limitations, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor; it provides smooth pedal assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem to custom-tune your riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for improved stopping power. For less than the cost of many unknown e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI’s warranty and service.

Salsa’s Moraine 145 costs less than many hardtail E-MTBs. But don’t let the price fool you; this bike is value-packed. This dual 29-inch-wheeled trail bike comes equipped with Fazua’s Ride 60 motor (60 Newton-meters of torque) and a 430-Watt-hour battery. While it has less torque and a smaller-capacity battery than higher-priced competitors, it has enough power for some serious fun in the woods and on singletrack.

The frame uses a Split Pivot suspension system designed by Dave Weagle (the mastermind behind the dw-link suspension system on Pivot bikes), for a balance of performance and pedalability. A 10-speed Shimano Cues drivetrain, four-piston Shimano brakes, a dropper post, and Terravail tubeless tires round out the components of this feature-packed full-suspension E-MTB.

Electric bikes are great for commuting and city life. However, their added weight (sometimes as much as 90 or 100 pounds) can make e-bikes a pain to carry up flights of stairs, load onto a bus or train, or even move around in your garage.

Weighing only about 40 pounds, the Roadster v3 cuts weight without sacrificing much performance or adding cost. Ride1Up uses a 500 watt/50Nm rear hub motor with an internal battery for a clean, stealthy look. 700x45c gravel tires carry speed on pavement or hardpack dirt roads, and metal fenders keep the road spray off your clothes.

Electric mountain bikes are a ton of fun and help you ride more of your favorite trails. We recommend full-suspension E-MTBs for aggressive and technical trails. But hardtails often work fine on easier trails and mellower terrain, and they cost a lot less than dual-suspension models.

Velotric keeps costs low on the Summit 1 by using a rear hub motor instead of a pricier mid-drive unit. The Summit also features an 8-speed Shimano drivetrain rather than more expensive 11- or 12-speed systems. However, Velotric gives the bike a 120mm thru-axle fork to soak up bumps, Shimano hydraulic disc brakes, and a full-color screen with Bluetooth connectivity.

Electric bikes are a great way for older riders to enjoy cycling and stay active. However, many commuter e-bikes have high top tubes, and even many step-through-style frames still require riders to swing their leg over the frame. The Velotric Discover has a Euro-style, low-step-through frame that makes it easier to get on and off.

Additional comfort features include an adjustable-rise stem, wide seat, and suspension seatpost. The Discover has a 28mph top speed and about 75 miles of range. At 63 pounds, it’s not super light, but it weighs less than many similarly priced e-bikes.

#9027. What’s the Minimum Amount of Mileage You Can Do to Maintain Fitness? Experts Answer

There’s one type of workout in particular that makes the biggest difference.

For some runners, taking a week or two off from running after a race is the hard part—they can’t wait to ramp back up their volume again. But for others, crossing a finish line (of any distance) might feel like a natural point to take a break from the sport, or at least to significantly scale back.

Still, if you trained for months to build up the fitness, including your aerobic capacity, lactate threshold, and running economy, you probably want to try to maintain at least some of that afterward. That way, you can go into a spring training cycle with a solid base.

Maintenance mode also gives you the flexibility to be able to jump into a 10K or half-marathon on a whim, says Mike Sheehy, running coach for Team Abbott who has completed more than 100 marathons.

Keeping a steady mileage base also allows you to experiment. “This gives you a chance to try new fuels, try new gear, a new pair of shorts, new pair of shoes, stuff you didn't like during your block,” Sheehy says. You could also experiment with pace. “This is a great block to think about moving your easy pace up 15 seconds to let your heart and body start adapting to that new norm.”

If you want to strike a balance between giving yourself a well-deserved break and completely reversing all of your gains, the question becomes: What’s the minimum running you can do to maintain your fitness? And how long can I do that without falling back?

Here’s what running coaches and an exercise physiologist have to say, plus what other forms of exercise come into play in the maintenance phase.

First, it’s important to note that taking a week or two off after a marathon and at least one week for the half is not only encouraged, it’s probably the best thing you can do for your body—and your mind.

“The thing I encourage all my runners to remember is patience,” says Sheehy. “Let your body heal and take that time.” He typically advises runners to take a full week off, then slowly add in easy miles without rushing to get back to quality workouts.

Then by the end of week two, you enter the true maintenance phase. “This is really an exciting time of running,” Sheehy says. “This is where we’re keeping 90 percent of the fitness with about 60 percent of the work.” He recommends taking the average mileage from your peak marathon training weeks rather than the single highest weekly mileage.

This tends to net out to between 20 and 30 miles a week in the maintenance phase for marathon runners and 10 to 15 miles a week for half-marathoners. That might look like three shorter, easier runs during the week and an 8- to 12-miler on the weekend. (Experts agree it’s best to run more frequently at lower volume for each run than do fewer, longer runs.) “That keeps you 90 percent fit, but allows you to enjoy running and not have the pressure of having to run six or five days a week and without having structured workouts,” Sheehy says.

Andrew M. Jones, Ph.D., professor of applied physiology at the University of Exeter in the U.K., puts the minimum effective dose of maintenance running slightly lower—at 50 percent—though after about four to six weeks at half the volume, runners will likely start to see “more significant deterioration,” he says, specifically of race-specific endurance. (Running economy may be more resilient.)

That’s not necessarily a bad thing (and allows you to focus on other goals; more on this soon), and 50 percent is enough to preserve a foundation to allow you to pick up at the beginning of a 16-week marathon training plan with relative ease.

Greg Laraia, a running coach at Motiv in New York City, agrees and provides this example: Say a runner finished Berlin on September 27 and plans to run London on April 24. After time off, he’d have them work back up to 50 percent of their mileage by October 25, then hover in the 50 to 60 percent of mileage range until early January when their London block would start in earnest.

Retaining intensity during the maintenance phase is arguably more important than frequency and duration, per Jones. “It’s impossible to give a minimum effective dose [for intensity] but ideally by week two [after a marathon] they’d get back to the pre-marathon training intensity but with lower volume,” he says, which might be lower duration and/or frequency of quality running. “Intensity is the key stimulus.”

To hit this stimulus, Sheehy and Laraia both like to have runners add in strides (e.g., four to six 30- to 60-second strides as part of an easy run) before doing more intense speed workouts that could make their way back into the weekly schedule about a month after a race.

Sheehy provides an example of a speed workout he likes to include during the maintenance phase:

“The new race pace is something I know they can achieve that is apparent in previous race results and workouts; not some aspirational wish pace,” Sheehy says. “This will give them the confidence they need or maybe a wake up call, but it makes for a great starting point, and allows us to calibrate their easy paces and use the lower volumes to let their body (and heart) adjust to the new norm.”

Sheehy cautions against swapping out runs that make up your maintenance mileage for other cardio, as it is important to maintain the specificity of running if you want to maintain running fitness. But he often adds in an indoor cycling day during his offseason on top of four or so days of running. If you dropped down your running frequency, an aerobic cross-training workout can support your fitness maintenance. Plus, it gives you a mental break, Jones says.

Laraia says one case where swapping maintenance miles for other cardio could make sense would be when runners come off a fall race injured or worn down and simply need a break from running so much. “Running is always going to be the best option because running is the sport, but if an elliptical or a bike is going to make you miss [running] enough to want to do it again, let’s start there,” he says.

The maintenance phase is also a great time to focus on strength training, Jones says. Sheehy agrees, suggesting aiming for two to three days a week. You can do more volume (either via an extra day or more sets/reps) during this phase, but it’s still important to include one true rest day in your plan, Sheehy says.

Strength work helps to build neuromuscular capacity, improve power that can translate to speed, and strengthen your tendons and ligaments for the upcoming season, especially if you focus on heavier lifting. “Let’s get comfortable with the extra load and then let’s see if it makes running better and more efficient,” Laraia says.

Laraia says signs that you may have pulled back too much include a higher-than-usual heart rate during runs or paces that feel harder than normal.

Still, it’s probably better to lose a little bit more running fitness in the offseason than to push yourself too hard, he says. The former is going to put you in a better position to start a new training block in the spring, compared with the latter, which could lead to burnout and could set your next training cycle back.

“Realistically, you’re going to be better off taking the extra day versus trying to push through something if you’re early in a block or just trying to maintain fitness,” Laraia says. “I’d rather you be 100 percent recovered for every run versus in the build,” where it might make sense to go into a run feeling a little depleted.

#9026. Is Your Body Fat Percentage Holding Back Your Cycling Goals? The Answer Depends on Your Age and Ambition.

Your body fat percentage is a tool, not a judgment. Here’s are the recommended ranges that cyclists can use to support their goals.

For cyclists, body composition is a critical performance factor that goes beyond aesthetics. It directly influences climbing speed, power endurance, and recovery capabilities. Average body-fat percentage averages and recommendations shift as we age depending on individual goals, and whether we’re a recreational rider or a competitive cyclist pursuing maximum power-to-weight ratio.

Understanding age and typical body fat percentage ranges gives us valuable context for setting realistic and healthy body composition goals and determining whether our focus should be on fat loss, strength building, or overall health. (It’s important to note that body fat percentage and BMI (body mass index) are not the same thing.)

🚴🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Cycling for Weight Loss program will help you find confidence and consistency in your training.

There isn’t a universally “right” body-fat percentage. Ideal targets depend on sex, age, activity level, and specific goals, in addition to whether you’re prioritizing general health, recreational fitness, or competitive performance. However, there are commonly used target ranges per decade that coaches, trainers, and sports scientists use as healthy guidelines (which should be treated as approximate).

Let’s examine “average” body fat percentages guidelines by decade, what the average body fat percentages are for men and women in the United States, and the impact of different measurement methods (DEXA scan, home body fat scale, InBody scan) on results. These averages should be regarded as benchmarks for setting achievable, performance-oriented goals, not as rigid targets. They serve as a navigational tool rather than a mandatory destination.

20s: Competitive athletes: 6–10 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 11–15 percent, Healthy range: 12–20 percent

30s: Competitive athletes: 7–11 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 12–16 percent, Healthy range: 14–22 percent

40s: Competitive athletes: 8–12 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 13–17 percent, Healthy range: 16–24 percent

50s: Competitive athletes: 9–13 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 14–18 percent, Healthy range: 18–26 percent

60+: Competitive athletes: 10–14 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 15–19 percent, Healthy range: 20–28 percent

20s: Competitive athletes: 14–18 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 19–23 percent, Healthy range: 20–30 percent

30s: Competitive athletes: 15–19 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 20–24 percent, Healthy range: 22–32 percent

40s: Competitive athletes: 16–20 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 21–25 percent, 50s: Competitive athletes: 17–21 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 22–26 percent, Healthy range: 26–36 percent

60+: Competitive athletes: 18–22 percent, Fit/recreational athletes: 23–27 percent, Healthy range: 28–38 percent

Cyclists specializing in climbing typically aim for the lower end of these ranges, though excessively rapid fat loss can compromise strength and power.

While the ranges above are recommended guidelines, the actual averages for folks according to the CDC look pretty different. The following data on average body fat percentage of men and women in the U. S. has been collected through the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey.

It’s important to note that the body fat percentage measurement method really matters. Home scales that measure body fat percentage can be quite inaccurate according to researchers. In my own experience, an InBody scan (which is the measurement method I recommend for a more reliable assessment, by the way) revealed that my body fat percentage is several percentage points higher than what the home body fat scale I have been testing had measured.

However, even InBody results can fluctuate with hydration levels. DEXA scans offer the most stable results but are generally more expensive. The key is to track trends over time rather than focusing on single numbers.

When it comes to fat loss, aim for a safe and healthy pace of 0.5-1 percent of body weight per week, while prioritizing preserving lean mass through optimal protein intake and strength training. However, it can be tricky to determine how much of the body weight lost is fat, and factors like how lean someone already is, a person’s metabolism, and training intensity also play a role.

As an example, in one study of female volunteers on reduced-calorie diets, participants were assigned exercise programs of varying intensity. According to the researchers, the women doing a moderate exercise program lost 6.2 percent body fat over three months on average, which added up to being about 2 percent a month. The intense exercise group lost an average of approximately 10 percent body fat over the same time period, which comes out to around 3.3 percent per month.

Understanding body composition is a valuable tool for cyclists looking to optimize their performance and achieve their goals. By considering your age, sex, activity level, and using reliable measurement methods, you can set realistic targets and tailor your training and nutrition strategies accordingly. Remember, it's all about finding the right balance for your body and your goals.

Natascha Grief is the fitness and reviews editor for Women’s Health. She writes about fitness, health, performance, everyday movement, and the products that help people train and recover better. She brings more than a decade of experience as a NASM-certified personal trainer focused on training women, with specialties in functional strength training, corrective exercise, nutrition, and behavior change. She previously worked as the health and fitness editor at Bicycling, and her writing has appeared in Runner’s World and other outlets. Across her work, she’s especially focused on making complex wellness, training, and performance topics approachable and accessible.

#9024. Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman)

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

Thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a new fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my big shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

After finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

“I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev said, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

“Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he said. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

“There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the plans because of those doubts.”

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

“That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that plan. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”

Sticking to the plan slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

“It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”

And for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

Physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

“To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

“It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

“You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

It worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

“I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before big races.”

The day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

“When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

“I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”

That feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

“It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”

Thankfully for him, time went by quickly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

After that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”

Recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”

Starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a new world’s best time, the specter of the Big Island tempered his elation.

“It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”

One of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his new, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev quickly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a big difference in how hot I feel.”

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of new cooling strategy.

“It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

“So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”

When you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

“We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”

A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

“Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he said, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev quickly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

“I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”

The bike offered another potential saving.

“My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”

For now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev says he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

“Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

“He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”
