#9022. 'I Ran 3 Miles A Day For 21 Days—Here's What I Learned About My Brain And Body'

Here’s what to expect, and how to commit.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

There’s something romantic about the idea of a daily run. It’s simple. It’s gritty. It’s giving “I can do hard things just because I believe I can,” main character energy. Plus, running three miles a day has become a bit of a fitness trend lately—just scroll through TikTok and you’ll see thousands of people sticking to that sweet-spot distance to get in shape, clear their heads, or just establish a healthy daily habit.

I’ve dabbled in running over the years (mostly during half-hearted attempts to train for a 10K or half marathon), but I’ve never been consistent. So I challenged myself: Run (at least) three miles a day, every day, for three weeks—no skips. I wanted to see if this simple habit could actually deliver real results: Physically. Mentally. Emotionally. To cut to the chase, it did.

But before we dive into exactly what I learned, here’s what the challenge I set out for actually entailed: Each day, I carved out 30-ish minutes to run a minimum of three miles—sometimes on the treadmill, sometimes outside, depending on my mood (and the weather). Sometimes fast, sometimes slow—I wasn’t chasing speed, just consistency.

And while it started out as a little personal experiment, it turned into a full-on mindset shift that seeped into other areas of my life.

I’m a pretty high-energy person, even on little sleep. And frankly, when I’m not exerting that physical energy enough during the day, I find it tough to settle down to sleep at night.

By week two of this challenge, I was zonking out faster than usual and waking up feeling more rested. Research backs this up—moderate aerobic exercise like running can help you fall asleep quicker and improve sleep quality, per the American Journal of Lifestyle Medicine.

There’s a reason running is considered a moving meditation (and I say this as someone who really struggles with stationary meditating). That ~30-minute mental break from work, life, communications, etc., helped me carve out time to shut off my brain and come back to reality with a fresh outlook.

Whatever I was stressing about before my run felt way less burdensome after taking time to move my body and just, well, not stress over that thing. I’d come back with more patience, more solutions, and frankly, a more can-do attitude about dealing with whatever was weighing me down before. My run became my reset button—and a way to make myself less irritable and more focused.

I’ve always gained (and lost) muscle pretty quickly after starting or stopping a new exercise routine, however I typically first notice it around my abs and arms, as I'm leaner in those regions. So, when I saw my calves and quads popping a bit more in the mirror, and climbing the four flights of stairs up to my apartment started feeling easier than it used to, I knew my body was adapting. Even though I wasn’t lifting weights during this three week challenge (I tried to at first, but decided it was too much for my schedule while also running three miles daily), the repeated use of lower-body muscles while running led to strength gains.

Going into this challenge, I expected a mental impact of some sort (though I wasn’t quite sure what it would be), but I didn’t think my body would change much from a short-distance, short-term running habit. I already work out often (switching it up with two to three weekly strength training sessions, yoga/pilates once per week, and a two to five mile run once per week), so I didn’t think this challenge would have a palpable physical effect on me. So, the lower body muscle and strength gains were by far the most surprising benefit I walked away with.

I’d never really consider myself a “runner,” but doing it daily for three weeks made the act feel less intimidating and more second nature to me. A study in Psychology of Sport and Exercise shows that consistency in movement creates more positive attitudes toward the habit, which makes you more likely to keep showing up. My experience totally backed that up.

Around day six, I felt myself gearing up for my run more instinctually—getting dressed, grabbing my headphones, keys, and lacing up my sneakers just right without having to think about it much. If on the first few runs I was moseying around the neighborhood walking for several blocks to put off actually starting the run, by week two I was excitedly hitting the pavement at my three-mile pace almost as soon as I got outside. Pacing myself began to feel more natural without checking my Nike Run Club app, and I started tapping into the sound of my feet hitting the concrete to gauge my effort.

Before this challenge, I had a habit of engaging in pretty critical self-talk on the regular. Also, mentally checking out mid-run was the norm in order to just get through it. My internal monologue when running used to be all about how much time was left, how uncomfortable I felt, or how nice it would feel to just stop. But sticking to a daily running habit triggered the kind of awareness and shift of self-talk that I’d been long overdue for. That mindset shift was probably the biggest win of all.

After a few days of three miles under my belt, I started celebrating tiny wins—like not stopping on a hill or picking up my pace on the final stretch. Instead of counting down the minutes or fixating on how slow I was moving, I was hyping myself up, which only propelled me further. Whether it was a solo sunset jog or a playlist-powered treadmill sesh, I always felt a little lighter—and a little more capable of not just enduring, but thriving through hard things—post-run. That energy and positive shift in self-talk started showing up in how I talked to myself outside of workouts, too.

It’s wild how one habit tends to have a domino effect, whether it’s constructive or destructive. Once I started running every day, I realized I wanted to support that effort outside of my run window. That meant reaching for water instead of a second coffee, getting in some light stretching at night, prioritizing protein in my meals, and actually winding down for sleep earlier than usual instead of binge-watching or doom-scrolling.

The momentum from running made other wellness choices feel less like chores and more like natural choices for self-care. I wasn’t trying to overhaul my entire routine overnight, but these little tweaks felt pretty intuitive, and really added up to help me stick with the challenge, and feel more energized and clear-headed throughout the day.

Okay, so full transparency: I didn’t just wake up one day and bust out 21 straight three-milers. I eased in by starting off slow to establish a new routine, and listening to my body along the way. Here’s how to start running three miles a day—without burning out.

Pro tip: “If you’re just starting out, alternate running days with walking or strength training to let your body adjust,” run coach Corky Corkum, CPT, previously told WH. “The number one reason new runners quit is injury or burnout from doing too much too soon.”

Want to try running three miles a day for yourself? These things made all the difference:

If your goal is to feel stronger, sleep better, and just feel a little more capable and confident—all with minimal equipment or cost—then yes, 100 percent. You don’t need a marathon medal to call yourself a runner or to be consistent. You just need a pair of sneakers, a bit of stick-to-it-ness, and a willingness to start where you are.

And if you happen to find yourself romanticizing the idea of making a daily jog a habit? I say lean into it.

These were the products I found myself consistently reaching for throughout my three week running challenge.

#9021. How to Find Stability and Freedom in Supported Headstand

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about Headstand first appeared in the July-August 1990 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

“Sthera sukham asanam,” “Posture is steady and comfortable,” says Patanjali in the first of his three sutras on asana. But as even experienced yoga students know, “steady and comfortable” are not the first words that come to mind to describe the sensation of standing on one’s head. And many couch potatoes would probably insist that they feel quite steady and comfortable as they sprawl out in front of the tube. So what exactly does Patanjali mean by the words sthira and sukham?

Because balancing in Headstand (Sirsasana) is such a challenge, it forces us to look deeply into our posture and our nervous system to discover an inner sense of balance. This interiorization of awareness can reveal some of the subtleties behind Patanjali’s words.

The word thira comes from the Sanskrit root tha, meaning “to stand,” which is also the root of the English words “stay,” “stable,” and “steady.” This root verb is of great importance in the Yoga Sutras. Patanjali first uses it in defining the term abhyasa, or practice, in Sutra I-13: “Practice is the endeavor toward stillness and stability of the mindfield.” According to Pandit Usharbhud Arya’s commentary, “Meditation means bringing the mind to stillness or stability, which means freedom from the rajasic and tamasic turbulences, the mind’s one-pointed concentration on a single sattic vrtti harmonious vibration remaining uninterrupted so that the mind flows in a calm, pacific, smooth stream.”

For a hatha yoga practitioner, the following question arises: How can I bring this level of mental stillness into an asana such as Headstand, and, conversely, how can I adjust in the asana to stabilize and deepen the mental stillness? In other words, how can I explore the states of thira and sukham in the pose?

In previous asana columns, we have looked at the relationship of the bones, the flesh, and the skin to posture, circulation, and breathing. We have seen that the muscle fibers assist in circulation through their pumping action and that when they are open to the free flow of the breath, they can subtly communicate with the inner lining of the skin. Stability and comfort are accompanied by stable, grounded bones, effortless breathing, a fluid feeling of the flesh, and a sensitive inner skin. Fear, insecurity, and instability, on the other hand, are accompanied by hardened muscles, disturbed breathing, restricted blood flow, collapsed joints, and insensitive skin. The question now becomes: How can I organize the bones, muscle fibers, and skin to create a stable posture that allows the breath and bodily fluids to flow freely?

Freedom or restriction of the breath and bodily fluids can be experienced in the expansion, contraction, and inner pressure of the body’s three main cavities: the pelvic-abdominal cavity (from the diaphragm to the pelvic floor), the thoracic cavity, and the skull. In any posture, the respiratory rhythm begins with an expansion of the thoracic cavity, accomplished by the contraction and descent of the diaphragm and the lifting and widening of the rib cage by the intercostal and other respiratory muscles. This expansion creates a negative pressure (lower than normal atmospheric pres sure) in the chest, drawing air from outside the body into the lungs. With the exhalation, a positive pressure (higher than normal atmospheric pressure) is created as the expansion ceases and the elastic recoil of the lung tissue presses the air out of the lungs.

In soft, quiet breathing, there is no resistance to this cycle. The pelvic-abdominal cavity expands and releases in harmony with the thoracic cavity, and air flows in and out of the body without impedence. The expansion and contraction of the body is perfectly matched by the movement of air in and out of the lungs. Because of this balance, the sensation of interior pressure remains constant throughout the body.

However, any unnecessary tension in the body will create resistance to the breath and a corresponding increase in resistance to the circulatory fluids. This resistance creates the sensation of increased internal pressure, a sensation to which the brain and skull are especially sensitive. To experience this sensation in an exaggerated way, inhale, close your mouth, close your nostrils with your fingers, and try to exhale.

Notice the immediate increase in pressure in the brain. Close your mouth and nostrils after exhaling and you will experience a slightly different pressure increase.

Tension anywhere in the body will have a similar pressurizing effect. For example, neck and shoulder tension restricts the expansion of the rib cage, disrupting the respiratory rhythm and increasing the pressure in the skull. Psychological stresses tend to be reflected in a tense diaphragm, and the diaphragm also reacts to tension in the groins and pelvic region. When the groins are open, the bones of the legs, pelvis, and lower spine support the weight of the body, and the muscles of that region are free to expand and contract with the breathing cycle. However, when the groins are restricted, the pelvic floor cannot

“breathe,” and this resistance in the pelvic-abdominal region impedes the movement of the diaphragm. This constriction of the breath creates pressure in the skull, just as you experienced when you held your mouth and nostrils shut.

Standing on one’s head exacerbates all of these restrictions to the breath. The shoulders and neck are often tensed to hold on to the body. Fears of falling tighten the diaphragm. The legs and pelvis are often collapsed and unconscious. Thus the breath will be constricted and the brain will feel pressurized. The most obvious aspect of this syndrome is that blood cannot move out of the skull, leading to a sense of congestion. (Some degree of pressure is usual when first starting to practice Headstand; a beginner should not expect to feel perfectly quiet and comfortable right away. But if the eyes become bloodshot or if extreme pressure is felt in the eyes or ears, the pose is being done incorrectly and should not be held. Seek guidance from a qualified teacher.)

The increased pressure in the skull results from a breakdown in the pumping system of the body. The diaphragm is a large pump for moving air, and the skeletal muscles must pump fluids back to the heart to maintain circulation. To facilitate these processes of circulation and respiration, the body is organized into six regions, each with its own “relay station” to oversee the movement of fluids and breath in and out of that region. Although most of these relay stations do not have a single specialized physical component like the diaphragmatic muscle, I will refer to them as diaphragms for lack of a better term, because, like the diaphragm, they function as pumps. (The term “diaphragm” is a convenient metaphor for the complex set of physiological and psychological mechanisms that control the movement of fluids, air, and energy in and out of a particular area of the body.

These diaphragms and their powerful effects can be experienced subjectively by turning the attention inward, although most of them cannot be objectively revealed through dissection.) These diaphragmatic regions, as introduced to me by my teacher, Ramanand Patel, are the brain, the throat, the heart, the respiratory diaphragm, the navel, and the pelvic floor.

In order to attain thira and sukham in Headstand, all six diaphragms must be functioning properly. However, this article will focus on the first and sixth diaphragm, as these are particularly important.

The sixth diaphragm has a tangible physical component, the muscles of the pelvic floor. Open groins, strong legs, and stable hip joints are necessary for the healthy functioning of this diaphragm, which should move synchronously with the physical diaphragm, creating the sense that the pelvis and abdomen breathe freely:

Correct action of the pelvic diaphragm stabilizes the coccyx bone and helps circulate fluids in and out of the legs. Its location is the first chakra, the chakra of grounding and stability, and thus it plays an important role in developing the quality of shira.

The first diaphragm is the brain or skull diaphragm, responsible for moving energy in the form of blood and cerebrospinal fluid) in and out of the brain. This diaphragm has no muscular components; rather, it is composed of a complex combination of neural pathways and blood vessels. My experience has been that it moves in opposition to the other five diaphragms: When the other five diaphragms are “inhaling,” or drawing energy in, the brain diaphragm is “exhaling,” or releasing. Conversely, when the lower five are exhaling, the brain “inhales.” This is the rhythm that accompanies a healthy nervous and circulatory system, leading to shira and sukham.

However, if the pelvic diaphragm is locked or inhibited, the brain diaphragm will “inhale” along with the torso, leading to an increase in tension in the muscles and pressure in the skull. This tension can also be felt as disturbances in the skin, eyes, ears, and tongue.

Before attempting Headstand, you should have a strong, stable Downward-Facing Dog Pose and a regular standing pose practice to ensure the strength, flexibility, and intelligence of your arms and legs necessary to protect the neck and skull. Use a firm blanket or mat for the head. If possible, learn to balance in a corner of the room, resting one foot on each wall to prevent tilting to one side or another. If a corner is not available, use any wall, placing your hands close to the wall to keep from arching your back into a banana shape.

Place your forearms on the floor, interlocking your fingers evenly and completely and keeping your wrists perpendicular to the floor. Your elbows should be exactly shoulder width apart. This foundation must be stabilized by constant practice.

In building this foundation, several difficulties may be encountered. One arm may overpower the other, distorting the shoulders, forearms, and wrists and torquing the foundation. Learn to press evenly into both arms. Your wrists may collapse outward, losing their grounding and strength. Consciously hold the thumb side of your wrists toward each other. Your elbows may splay apart. Maintain a constant pressure from your outer elbows toward each other, as if your elbows were pressing into a block held between them. However, do not draw them closer than shoulder width.

Having established this stable foundation, place your head up against your wrists and palms, cupping your skull without losing the strength of the wrists. Taking the weight onto the arms and not the neck, use the strength of the groins and pelvis to lift both legs up from the floor. (Beginners will probably have to throw one leg up at a time, but as soon as possible should begin lifting both at once.) Resting your feet against the wall, lift the weight of the body out of the shoulders, away from the neck.

Learning this lifting action is more important than learning to balance. Only when the lift is strong and the balance stable should you move to the center of the room.

Students who can balance steadily in the center of the room can begin to explore the effect on the pose of the pelvic and brain diaphragms. Most beginning students look something like the “inverted banana” in Figure 1. Your shoulders sink, the floating ribs and upper lumbar hang forward, your back body collapses, and your legs fall behind the midline. With no vertical extension, the weight of the torso collapses onto your neck and skull, compressing the brain diaphragm. The legs are not lifting, and their weight hardens the posterior pelvic floor and the inner front groins. The anterior coccyx bone hangs unsupported.

Instead, your arms and shoulders must lift actively away from the neck and skull. Figure 2 shows a close-up of the correct lifting action. Note the widening of the upper inner shoulder blades and the lifting of the inner and outer deltoid muscles, which lifts the weight of the torso away from the neck and skull. This action can be learned in Downward-Facing Dog (Adho Mukha Svanasana).

Your legs also must be brought forward, lifting the lumbar, pelvis, and legs to eliminate the banana-like collapse. Intermediate students often learn this action, only to close the anterior pelvis and inner groins and lose the support of the posterior coccyx (see Figure 3). The front and inner groins must be dynamically extended, without collapsing onto the lumbar. Your legs must work tremendously in Headstand to open the pelvic diaphragm. In working the legs, be sure to extend the bones from the pelvis without hardening and tensing the muscles—rather, keep the muscles vibrant. If the leg muscles harden, the pelvic diaphragm will tighten and the brain will become pressurized and confused.

In the completed position (Figure 5), your front body and back body extend evenly, aligning the bones with gravity. When the bones are aligned, they can support the weight of the body without muscular strain. Figure 4 has been inverted to show the alignment of the arches, knees, hips, shoulders, and ears. By lifting evenly out of the pelvis, the bones of the legs free the pelvic diaphragm to breathe and pump blood to the legs. The dynamic action of the legs lifts the weight of the torso from the skull, allowing the brain diaphragm to breathe.

The anterior and posterior sides of the coccyx bone are supported, freeing the pelvic diaphragm. This freedom allows the respiratory diaphragm to breathe easily, which in turn allows the brain to feel relaxed and spacious. Thus the whole pose feels spacious, stable, and comfortable.

Stability and comfort are prerequisites for deeper work in the poses. As Vyassa says in his commentary to the first of the Yoga Sutras, yoga is samadhi. Sthira and sukham are the beginning of the samadhi state and thus are the point at which true yoga commences. All previous action is preparatory in nature. To achieve thira and sukham, it is not sufficient just to sit in any comfortable pose. Rather, you must perfect the pose to such an extent that samadhi can spontaneously awaken.

The universe is alive, awakening and creating itself anew with each moment. If we create the proper foundations of shira and sukham, so that our mind and body are clear and calm, we can directly experience this awakening and creativity. With 10 years until the turn of the millenium, human consciousness is awakening to its own inner potentials as it is simultaneously awakening to the potentials of the natural world. All serious practitioners of yoga should work to be stabilized at least in the beginning level of thira and sukham by then, so we can usher in a new age of planetary awakening, with wisdom, compassion, and ecological communion with the natural world as our goals.

#9020. Garmin LiveTrack Now Alerts Waze Drivers to Nearby Cyclists

Opt-in LiveTrack sharing puts a moving cyclist icon in Waze and alerts some nearby drivers.

Rearview radars are one of our favorite cycling accessories because they alert riders when a vehicle is approaching from behind. Now Garmin and Waze are flipping that warning around: Their new partnership alerts drivers when a cyclist using Garmin’s LiveTrack is nearby.

Here’s how it works. Start an outdoor cycling activity with LiveTrack on a compatible Garmin Edge computer or smartwatch, and your location will appear in Waze as a moving cyclist icon. Drivers don’t need to be navigating a route to see cyclists; Waze told me the icons appear whenever the app is open, as riders enter the driver’s broader route area or immediate surroundings.

Waze says the alert comes when a cyclist gets closer, but it hasn’t specified the distance. In an email response to my questions, Garmin told me alerts go to “relevant drivers,” usually when the rider and driver are on the same road and traveling in the same direction. A cyclist farther ahead on the driver’s mapped route may also trigger one.

If several riders are together, Waze shows one icon to avoid repeat alerts. If they spread out, multiple icons appear. Garmin describes the grouping feature as “built-in clustering logic.”

For Waze users, cyclist alerts are on by default but can be turned off in the app’s settings. Riders opt in to Waze sharing through Garmin, but only once. After that, sharing starts whenever they begin a cycling LiveTrack, whether they start it manually or set it to start automatically.

Garmin says any Edge computer or smartwatch with LiveTrack is compatible. LiveTrack requires a phone paired with Garmin Connect and cellular coverage; Garmin’s LTE-enabled devices can run LiveTrack without relying on the phone’s connection.

No additional subscription or purchase is required. Waze says drivers see only a temporary alert that a cyclist is nearby, not the rider’s name, identity, or exact route. Sharing stops when the ride ends.

This is not V2X, the connected-vehicle technology that has been simmering in the background. V2X systems let vehicles exchange information with one another, roadside infrastructure, and other road users, including cyclists. Garmin and Waze are taking an app-based route to a similar goal: LiveTrack sends a rider’s location to Waze, which can alert drivers using the app.

It’s a sensible idea, but it requires the latest apps and firmware, a Garmin rider who has opted in, a working connection, and a driver using Waze. It isn’t a substitute for cycling-friendly infrastructure, and it won’t fix distracted drivers or jerks in cars. But reminding drivers that cyclists are on the road is a step in the right direction.

Would you enable Waze sharing for your LiveTrack rides? If you use Waze while driving, would a cyclist icon or alert change how you approach the road? Tell us in the comments, or join me on Discord. I’d especially like to hear from riders who already use LiveTrack or Waze: What would you want to know before turning this on?

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#9017. A Runner Took a Midrace Puff of Weed at the NYC Marathon. Now, She’s Disqualified.

This Houston attorney lost her official result, but kept her medal—and her sense of humor.

Having your first marathon result erased after months of training might be enough to send anyone into a downward spiral. Andrea Sager, though, has been getting some serious mileage out of the bad news on Instagram.

"Damn, I can't send my 5:54 to Boston now 💀," the 35-year-old joked in a recent post, referencing the news that she’d been disqualified from the 2026 NYC Marathon despite crossing the finish line.

The Houston attorney and mother of two found out she was DQ’d days after the November 1 race when footage surfaced of her smoking marijuana on the course. The moment she decided to accept a puff from a spectator was caught on video, and New York Road Runners subsequently removed her finish time from its records.

As far as the rules go, there's little room for debate. NYRR's Code of Conduct explicitly prohibits "smoking, vaping, or use of electronic smoking devices, tobacco products, or marijuana products" in the starting corrals, on the course, and in the finish area, with the restriction extending 1,000 feet beyond those locations.

In a video explaining her disqualification, Sager acknowledged breaking the rules and said she understood the decision. Even so, she claimed she wasn’t the only runner to drink alcohol or smoke weed during the race, and suggested the difference was having the moment seen by millions of people on social media.

"I wasn't planning on smoking weed on the course, but I was in so much pain and needed something to help me finish," she told the New York Post.

Sager hasn't let the penalty spoil her memories of race day. Her original finish-line recap described a grueling 26.2 miles that involved "approximately 47 mental breakdowns," although she was thrilled to check the race off her bucket list. She later reminded followers that the experience could not be taken away from her.

She'd been having plenty of fun long before arriving in New York, too. One prerace Instagram video joked about giving up dating apps in favor of training for a marathon, while her bright pink marathon shirt doubled as a personal advertisement. The front read, "Andrea, 35, Single. Great Credit. Bad Judgment," while the back added, "Looking for a man with more endurance than my ex."

Her latest social media introduction has since acquired another word: "35. Single. Great credit. Poor judgment. Disqualified."

Sager still has her finisher medal, and the extra attention has brought some unexpected opportunities.

"I'm talking with the brands now, so there's a lot of upside, but still annoying," she told the Post.

Sager said she was told she can participate in future NYRR events, despite the removal of her November 1 result. Runner's World contacted the organization for comment and confirmation of her eligibility but received no response.

As for racing plans, Sager said she has HYROX Houston on her calendar for April 2027. And someone in her Instagram comments has suggested a shirt idea for her next event:

"I smoked weed at the NYC marathon and all I got was a DQ."

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#9016. The Bivo Trio Mini Keeps Finding a Place on Our Bikes When the Temperatures Begin to Dip—Here’s Why

In a crowded category, the Bivo Trio Bottle ends up in our bottle cages for colder rides.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Your water bottles have probably frozen at least once if you ride outside in cold weather. Usually, it’s only a thin layer of ice on top or a clogged nozzle, but that’s enough to be annoying. If you ride at low enough temperatures with standard plastic bottles filled with plain water, it will inevitably happen. However, it’s important to stay hydrated on winter rides.

There are proven ways to keep your bottles from freezing—or carry hot beverages on rides. Hot chocolate, coffee, tea, or Skratch Labs’ apple cider will warm your soul and lift your mood. And nothing hits better than a coffee stop in the middle of a cold winter ride, especially when conditions are dreary or sloppy.

Stainless insulated bottles broke into cycling about five years ago and have since exploded in popularity. They’re a proven way to keep water and hydration mix cool on the hottest summer days, and they can also keep hot drinks warm for many miles on winter rides.

The Bivo Trio Bottle, available in raw stainless steel and silicone-covered stainless steel versions, has become a bottle of choice on cold-weather rides. Read on to find out why, plus tips to prevent your bottles from freezing this winter.

Cyclists have many different methods (often handed down from one generation of riders to the next) to help prevent frozen bottles. One simple solution is to start your ride with hot water. However, depending on the temperature and ride length, this can also freeze.

Using insulated plastic bottles, adding a high-sodium drink mix, and wearing a hydration pack or vest under a riding jacket are all tricks I’ve used (with varying degrees of success) to keep my bottles from freezing. And some riders still swear by adding a shot of booze to their bidon. However, while these methods may prevent icing, they still result in a cold beverage during your ride.

It’s hard to miss the growing popularity of stainless steel water bottles in cycling. Their use has boomed in the last few seasons as more riders have become concerned about microplastic contamination. Plus, these metal bidons, particularly the Bivo bottles, are in the cages of many cycling influencers.

Stainless bottles typically feature a vacuum-sealed double-wall design with a coated outer and a bare stainless inner layer. Since metal bottles are rigid, you cannot squeeze them like plastic bottles. (It takes some getting used to if you haven’t ridden them before.) And while stainless bottles are much heavier than plastic models, they are heavy-duty and almost indestructible—they dent and scratch but rarely break.

Bivo is the trend-setting stainless option and commonly available from retailers like REI, Backcountry, Amazon, or your local bike shop. The Insulated Mini we tested is 17 ounces and costs $44, or opt for the 21-ounce model for $5 more.

I have ridden with insulated bottles at several points in my cycling life. But until last summer, I usually stuck with non-insulated plastic bottles for most of my rides, regardless of air temperature.

Generally, I prefer the feel of a regular bottle; 22-ounce Specialized Purist bottles are my go-to, and I occasionally carry a 10-ounce Purist Maker mug for a mid-ride coffee break. But I often skip stainless insulated bottles because they aren’t squeezable and weigh noticeably more than plastic bidons.

However, before a recent ride on a cold and blustery day, I filled an insulated bottle with hot chocolate and was pleased to have a warm treat throughout my 90-minute ride. So, like my insulated bottle test last summer, I applied a little science to see which insulated stainless bottles performed best in cold temps.

For this test, I gathered several popular metal insulated bottles. First, I evaluated the bottles by measuring water temperature over three hours in subfreezing conditions. Then, I used them on rides in cold weather to determine which worked best from a functional perspective.

While the intent was somewhat scientific, I also strove to be practical—these are tests anyone can do at home. This testing was not performed in a controlled environment or with professional-level, calibrated equipment.

Since it was below 32 degrees outside, I was able to perform outdoor freeze testing. Like my summer insulated bottle tests, I filled the selected bottles with 400 grams of tap water (heated to 212 degrees for this test instead of chilled water used in summer). Then I placed the filled bottles on my front porch in subfreezing temperatures; I did this after sunset so sunlight would not warm the bottles. Every 30 minutes, I checked and recorded the water temperature of each bottle, in the same order each time, with a digital food thermometer.

Following the initial three-hour test period, the bottles remained overnight in sub-freezing temperatures for an additional nine hours. This tested whether the contents would stay warm for a full 12 hours (as per some bottle makers’ claims). Additionally, for reference, I subjected a Purist Maker tumbler (with 200 grams of water), an insulated plastic bottle, and a standard plastic bottle to the same tests.

The following day, I evaluated the bottles’ on-bike performance on a short loop in my neighborhood. I tested their use with standard and lobster-claw gloves (such as holding, opening caps, removing them from cages) and their nozzles’ function while drinking hot coffee (a medium-roast pour-over with some oat milk for my tests 😉).

The results were clear: Insulated stainless bottles work very well in cold weather. They keep your beverage hot for an hour-long ride in 30-degree temps. For longer rides, your drink will experience some heat loss but will remain drinkably warm for three hours. The insulated metal bottles performed notably better than plastic bottles (insulated and non-insulated) for the full duration of the test.

After about three hours of exposure in the cold, the Bivo Insulated Trio Mini kept my coffee at a warm 119.8 degrees. This is only slightly below coffee expert James Hoffmann’s recommended coffee-drinking temp of 122 to 129 degrees. (Although I’m not sure Hoffmann would be pleased drinking three-hour-old brew.) In 12-hour testing, none of the metal bottles froze. Most bottles finished at room temperature after 12 hours outside in freezing temperatures.

On the bike, the Bivo valve works great, and the bottle texture isn’t overly slippery. The bottle shape is compatible with most cages, though it fits best in the Arundle Sport cage recommended by Bivo.

Nozzle Shield: Look for bottles with a cap that protects the nozzle. Typically, I’m not a fan of these shields when riding in warm weather—they flop around and get in the way when drinking. However, in the winter, caps keep road salt and slush off the bottle’s nozzle, and they also help prevent icing. Ones with a removable plastic or rubber shield are easier to clean; plus, you can use the bottles without the cap on warm days.

Vapor Pressure: Many of the tested bottles carry a warning about using liquids hotter than 180 degrees. This is to avoid scalding and burns from pressurized hot water when the cap or nozzle is opened. With insulated bottles, hot liquid heats the air inside the bottle enough to spray potentially near-boiling water into your mouth or onto your body.

Avoid this by letting your hot beverage cool slightly before pouring it into your bottle. For long rides (when using two bottles of hot drinks), save the hotter bottle for later in the day. This way, it has time to cool to a drinkable temperature.

Cage Compatibility: Since they do not deform or flex, metal bottles don’t pair with every bottle cage. Some stainless bottles have a loose fit in cages (bottles can even eject on rough roads), and some cage shapes do not allow some metal bottles to sit correctly, causing annoying rattling and buzzing while riding. Other cage-bottle pairings are so tight that it’s hard to remove the bottle while riding.

My advice: Check that your cages work before dropping up to $100 for new bottles that won’t fit. Some brands have specific cage recommendations on their sites. You can also read user reviews for the compatibility of different bottles and cages. Also, be sure to check the overall bottle height to be sure it fits in your frame.

Dropped Bottles: I do not recommend using metal bottles in mass-start situations; use plastic bidons for big group rides or races. When a metal bottle is ejected from a cage on a bump, or you drop one (as is prone to happen with cold hands or when wearing bulky gloves), it ricochets off the road surface more than a plastic bottle. And while metal makes these bottles more durable, they do not burst open on impact or crush if hit by other riders.

Bivo shook up the bottle market when it launched its stainless steel bottles. The small Richmond, Vermont-based company launched insulated bottles shortly after, and cyclists have fallen in love with them. They work well, look good, and don’t have a funky taste.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#9015. This is What Happens When You Slow Down Long Enough to Be Curious

It’s one thing to know you need to slow things down in your everyday experience of life—to slow your thoughts, your breath, your attention, your scrolling, even your assumptions. It’s an entirely different thing to know how to slow down. Longtime mindfulness teacher, yoga therapist, and author Jillian Pransky addresses that disconnect in her recent book, The Power of the Pause: 90 Seconds to Calm, Reset, and Reconnect. In its pages, she explains exactly how pausing can alchemize everyday interactions in ways you’ve probably never considered. The following excerpt from the “Pausing in Our Discomfort Zone” chapter shows how slowing down can help you experience a more nuanced understanding of not only yourself but those who approach the world from a different perspective than you—and why that can benefit everyone. —Renee Marie Schettler, Editor in Chief, YJ

Neuroscientists tell us that life changes at the end of our comfort zone. The ability to build new neural pathways is called neuroplasticity, and it happens not only from repeating “new” behaviors, but also when we reach beyond what we know and explore new territories. Whether learning a new skill or facing a fear, your brain actively creates new neural connections, enhancing cognitive abilities, memory, and overall brain health.

However, we often decide in advance how things will go, or assume we know how another person is feeling. These assumptions can keep us stuck in patterns of behaviors or relationship dynamics that simply strengthen our resistance to change. When we remind ourselves that we have space to change, we often begin to see that there might be more going on than we think. We can open up to paradox, contradiction, and complexity in ways we were not able to before.

We may realize that no way is the only way. That we don’t need to make anything one way. And that things don’t always have to be precisely the way we want them.

Pausing helps us create support and safety for ourselves, giving us the confidence and courage to go beyond our comfort zone. Gradually titrating, step-by-step, into new territory allows our brain to integrate these changes, leading to our personal growth and evolution.

Dr. Gail Parker, psychologist, international presenter, and author of the self-care book Restorative Yoga for Ethnic and Race-Based Stress and Trauma, emphasizes that curiosity is essential for opening space in our conversations for connection, particularly among disparate groups of people.

She says, “You can make someone else feel safe when you are curious rather than judgmental, assuming, or indifferent. In the face of listening to others, especially those we don’t know so well or those from another culture, it’s important to remember that we can’t know everything about others or every culture, but what we can do is be curious about others.”

Listening includes being aware of ourselves and how we feel while conversing with another. In this way, we can learn to notice our own expectations and emotions, stay curious about ourselves, and hold space for ourselves and the other person. Dr. Parker suggests Pausing to check in with ourselves during conversations, with questions like:

• Am I truly listening? • Am I making assumptions? • Do I have expectations? • What am I feeling?

If we can stay aware of ourselves and curious about our feelings, we won’t get stuck in what we are feeling. “A key to remember is that if we can notice when we are in the stress response, we are not stuck in it,” she says.

Hala Khouri, author of several books, co-editor of Practicing Liberation: Transformative Strategies for Collective Healing and Systems Change, and co-founder of the social activism organization Off the Mat, Into the World, also emphasizes curiosity as an essential cornerstone for connection in difficult conversations.

Khouri, who is also a therapist, yoga teacher, and somatic experience practitioner, contends that curiosity is not only a portal for going deeper into our conversations, but is also the key to helping us know when it is time to leave a conversation—or not have one at all.

“When we are in conversation with another, I think it is important to ask ourselves, can I be curious right now? If we can’t get curious, that might be a good indicator that we need a break or need to remove ourselves from the conversation or situation, if that is an option,” she says.

The main point is that we need to stay connected to ourselves so we can sense our internal state. True listening requires curiosity. If we can’t be curious, that’s essential information for us. And, when we are highly activated in the stress response, we cannot simultaneously be curious. That part of our brain is not accessible when we are in fight-or-flight mode.

Whenever you notice you can’t be curious, take a moment to Pause and care for yourself until you can get your curiosity back.

If we could consciously choose to enter conversations with the intention to Listen—to be curious—to understand the other person’s experience a little bit better, maybe even put ourselves in their shoes, we might be able to learn from people in our lives whose world views are different from ours or even opposed to ours.

It can be helpful to remember that leading with curiosity rather than certainty doesn’t automatically mean that someone else is right. Or that we are wrong. But it opens a space in which we might connect rather than shut down to each other. The goal is not necessarily to reach agreement with others, but to understand each other. For many, this is a radical idea.

Dr. Parker emphasizes that harmonious relationships require awareness, not agreement. In fact, insisting on an agreement can be a hostile act. She says that the search for agreement can often lead to arguments because it invalidates the other person’s perspective, whereas the search for understanding dissolves the barriers that result in discord and harm and allows us to get to know one another.

She explained it like this: “If I need to be right, then I’m not going to be able to listen to you unless you are in agreement with me. And, if I need to be right, it means either you have to agree with me or you’re wrong. The need to be right means that somebody else has to be wrong. Who likes to be wrong? Nobody. Nobody wants to be made to feel like they’re wrong. Making someone wrong will most likely push them into a protective stance. But, when we approach someone with curiosity, it creates a whole new opening to make a connection with each other. We might say to them, ‘Tell me more…I’m really interested in that…I never thought about it that way.’”

When we are in difficult or uncomfortable conversations, can we create space to listen to each other with our differences? Can we create space for communication and connection for its own sake rather than for someone to be right and another to be wrong? How can we learn to understand each other rather than agree? How can we treat each other (and ourselves) better while learning to better understand each other and our different perspectives?

Pausing with the intention to prioritize Listening before speaking helps us regulate our nervous system so that we can not only create this space, but we are also less likely to activate someone else’s stress response. Khouri says, “Imagine two nervous systems on high alert trying to have a conversation, it’s almost impossible! Especially if both parties are vying for being right. If you want to disrupt that pattern, you need to figure out how to self-regulate; part of that is about tolerating the discomfort of disagreeing with someone or being in conflict.”

“One of the most interesting things I’ve discovered in my work, is that when people feel really, really listened to, they themselves are more willing to try to understand the other person, even when they don’t agree,” continues Khouri. “Through this type of listening, I’ve seen some people with very strong convictions and beliefs loosen their grip on their own fixed ideas and start to open up their perspective or get greater understanding and empathy for a different perspective.”

If we can Pause during a contentious situation and shift into curiosity, we might stay in the conversation long enough to ask questions that help us get to know someone, and listen in a way that makes them feel genuinely heard. When people feel heard and acknowledged, they are more likely to feel safe enough to listen in return. If we want to be heard and understood, it often starts with ensuring that the other person feels heard first. This of course takes practice.

Excerpt reprinted with permission from The Power of the Pause by Jillian Pransky © 2026. Published by Union Square & Co., an imprint of Hachette Book Group.

#9014. Procrastinating Your Winter Runs? Here’s What Will Actually Get You Out the Door, According to a Sports Psychologist

An expert explains which strategies work, what backfires in the long term, and when procrastination signals you need a training reassessment.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Nine months of the year, I rarely struggle to get myself out the door for a run. Then winter arrives, the temperatures drop, and suddenly it’s three straight months of daily prerun procrastination: I look for any excuse, task, or chore to delay heading out into the cold or stepping on the treadmill.

While this does have occasional productivity benefits—my kitchen floor shines and my email inbox stays at zero—I’ll find myself more than an hour later no closer to starting my run. Except by then, I’m crunched for time, it’s pitch-black outside, and the whole process has drained enough of my mental energy that I’d rather push those miles to tomorrow.

I know I’m not alone: Even professional marathoners fall into the “run-crastination” spiral. Previously, Des Linden and Kara Goucher discussed their own experiences on their podcast, Nobody Asked Us with Des & Kara. Still, I’d much rather find a way to avoid getting sucked in so I can get on with my run and my day, and enjoy both a little more as a result.

So, I asked a sports psychologist what actually works to get you out the door in the winter when anything sounds better than a run—plus when it’s actually a better idea to skip the miles.

The first step to beating prerun procrastination? Determine the reason you’re doing it. “Procrastination is usually one of two things,” Justin Ross, Psy.D., a clinical sports psychologist and UESCA-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World. “One: It’s an avoidance strategy, because what you’re about to do is uncomfortable, unpleasant, hard, or challenging. But, it can also signal toward a different need that’s not being met.”

In the winter months—especially for driven runners coming off a fall marathon season—that other need can be rest. “True athletic wisdom is knowing the difference between when procrastination is avoidance, and when it’s a sign that you need something other than a run that day,” Ross explains.

Gaining that wisdom as an athlete takes time, practice, and some trial and error. The best way to start? Focus on creating “systems” that make procrastination less likely so you can more easily identify the action that aligns with your needs, goals, and values, Ross says. Most times, these systems (which we outline below) lead to better outcomes than trying to rely on willpower alone or following an impulse in the moment.

If you find yourself avoiding a run, remove as many obstacles as possible that stand between you and getting out the door or to the gym. For Ross, that means setting out all his running clothes and fuel ahead of time so he doesn’t need to hunt for that one pair of gloves he hasn’t seen since last January.

“Without preparation, procrastination becomes a whole lot easier because you have all these extra hurdles,” he explains. “When it’s dark and cold in the winter, you need to problem-solve in ways that you don’t need to when it’s beautiful out and you’re excited to run.”

For me, that means making sure my headlamp actually has working batteries if I’m planning to run outside in the evenings. If I’m hitting the treadmill, I cue up a playlist, TV show, or podcast on my phone and stock my gym bag with a postrun snack and a full water bottle.

When you’re procrastinating a run, try shifting your focus from what you’re doing to why you’re doing it. “Remind yourself why this run is important to you or how it helps you,” Ross says. For example, you might think about your values or current goals and consider how this workout brings you closer to them.

I’ve found I’m motivated simply by the fact that running makes me feel like my favorite version of myself—and that boosts my mood more than any race-specific or fitness goal. But you might be more excited by the idea that staying consistent with your training over the winter will set you up for a stronger chance at a marathon PR in the spring.

Consider what might add a little bit more spark to your routine or make it more enticing. You might decide to meet up with a friend or local run club for a few miles. You might look forward to your treadmill run as “the 30 minutes of my day where I don’t have to be bothered and I can just watch my favorite show [alone],” says Ross.

The reward mindset helps you refocus on what brings you joy, instead of just relieving the pressure of needing to get in a workout.

Another helpful strategy? Doing the absolute bare minimum. “Runners often fall into this trap of having rigid rules around their exercise or their training,” says Ross. Try letting go of whatever mileage or workout you had planned for the day, and tell yourself that you’ll just run for 10 minutes and then reassess how you feel.

You may even want to adjust your whole training standard ahead of the winter season, Ross says. For example, you might reduce the length, intensity, or frequency of the workouts you plan to do each week. Or, instead of targeting a specific pace or mileage requirement, run or cross-train solely based on time. “Think about being more flexible in your approach during the winter months. Maybe you aim for the minimal effective dose to get the benefit you’re looking for, like just running for 20 minutes if your usual standard is 60,” Ross suggests.

Ross explains that winter can be a meaningful time for runners to examine what rules they have around their training that might be adding pressure. For example, I used to follow a silly rule from an old college teammate who said that any run shorter than three miles “didn’t count” as a true run. Once I finally let go of that, I found it much easier to get moving—even if it was just for an easy walk in the park near my house.

“This time of year, see how you can approach exercise from an overall health or mood-boost perspective instead of a training perspective,” suggests Ross.

Also, question any rigid rules you’ve established for yourself around volume, pace, or mileage—like making sure to hit a specific number of miles every week or setting a minimum pace requirement for all your runs—because they may backfire and lead to mental burnout over the long term, he says.

If you’ve done all the above and you still can’t get yourself out the door, a run may not actually be what you need. “If you keep hitting the moment to head out and that intuitive voice says, ‘I just really don’t want to,’ try listening to that voice. Listen to your body,” Ross suggests. “It’s okay to give yourself permission for rest and recovery—especially during this time of year.”

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#9013. Isakova and Hidalgo Win Final WTCS Races in Abu Dhabi, Jorgensen Podiums

The postponed WTCS Abu Dhabi brought the World Triathlon Championship Series, as it is currently known, to a close ahead of its transition to T50 racing within the Triathlon World Tour. The sprint-distance showdown still attracted many of the sport’s top names, with Olympic qualification points and the chance to finish the season on a high and build momentum into 2027.

The top spot on the podium was wide open in the women’s race, with the series’ undefeated champion Cassandre Beaugrand (FRA) absent. Add to the mix the shorter, sprint-distance format and hot, windy conditions set to play a factor, and it was anyone’s guess who would take it.

2025 world champion Lisa Tertsch (GER) was the big name going in, alongside Jeanne Lehair (LUX), who had been part of a sprint finish at the World Cup in Hong Kong the week before. However, Diana Isakova (RUS) was another athlete many had their eyes on after winning that sprint against Lehair and taking the World Cup win in Rome before that. American Gwen Jorgensen (USA) had shown glimmers of top form in recent races, placing fifth at WTCS Weihai and producing the second-fastest run split at the Grand Final in Pontevedra.

Into the warm, 82-degree water, three groups began to form near the front as the chop and currents made for one of the most difficult swims of the year.

Isakova and Lehair were among the first group out of the water, while Tertsch and Jorgensen exited more than 20 seconds behind. That deficit would quickly balloon to over 30 seconds early on the bike, with another group between them and the front of the race.

Halfway through the bike, the front group of nine maintained its advantage as the third group swallowed the second to form one large chase pack. On such a tight, technical course, the larger group offered little additional benefit as the smaller pack ahead steadily increased its lead.

At the end of the bike, Germany’s Laura Lindemann (GER) almost undid the work of the front, mishandling her bike after the dismount, almost causing a crash. Onto the run, a quick transition shot Isakova to the front, while around 36 seconds behind, Jorgensen and Tertsch were among the large group with significant work to do – and only 5km to do it.

By halfway, Isakova and Lehair were clear at the front, foreshadowing a repeat of the race in Hong Kong the week prior. Jorgensen remained 36 seconds behind but had gapped Tertsch and made her way into eighth place.

That momentum continued for Jorgensen as suddenly eighth place became third and she could see the leaders up ahead. Unfortunately, the gap was just too large at that point. Isakova made her move with over 200 meters to go, picking up her first WTCS win and cementing her remarkable end to the year.

Lehair finished second and reflected that her efforts on the bike may have affected her run: “I may have used too much energy, but I am super happy with second place and my third podium of the year.”

Jorgensen couldn’t believe her result, returning to the WTCS podium for the first time since 2016 at 40 years old and producing the fastest run split of the day.

“I thought I was out of this race but one of the coaches told me I was third and I couldn’t believe it,” she shared.

In the men’s race, this year’s Grand Final winner and sprint-distance specialist Matt Hauser (AUS) was wearing bib #1. With his prowess in the water, all eyes were on him in the absence of new world champion Vasco Vilaça (POR). Brazil’s Miguel Hidalgo (BRA), meanwhile, was looking to finally turn his training form into a result after some disappointing recent outings.

New Zealand’s Hayden Wilde (NZL) was the other big name on the lineup, having recently been approved to race both WTCS Abu Dhabi and Dubai T100. With the races falling within 24 hours of each other, that would not normally be allowed under World Triathlon rules. With his eyes firmly back on the Olympics, this was Wilde’s A-race for the weekend, according to New Zealand’s National Performance Manager Stephen Sheldrake.

It started with a windy, choppy swim that mostly stayed compact until the return to the beach, when two lines formed toward the shore. One group, including Hauser, made a beeline for the beach to get out of the water as soon as possible and run along the shore toward transition. That worked well for the Australian, who entered T1 with a small gap over compatriot Luke Willian (AUS).

Wilde found himself 39 seconds in arrears, with work to do alongside recent Iquique World Cup winner David Cantero del Campo (ESP). They were in a large chase group aiming to gain time on the lead group of 11, but on such a short, fast, five-lap bike course, their work was cut out for them.

Almost immediately, however, the gap was nearly cut in half, with Wilde driving the chase to within 22 seconds by the end of the first lap. The pace was so hot that the group split apart, with only a few athletes able to go with him on the technical course.

Perhaps that woke up the front group, which managed to limit its losses over the remainder of the bike and reached T2 with around nine seconds on Wilde and company. It was less than they would have hoped for against the stellar Kiwi runner, but the big question was whether the bike had stung his legs enough to hold him off. A slow transition from the 2025 winner of this race gave him even more work to do.

Onto the run, it didn’t take long for Hauser and Hidalgo to separate themselves at the front. Behind them, Wilde quickly recovered from his transition losses and moved through the rest of the front group alongside Shachar Sagiv (ISR).

The front two continued to push the pace and began adding time to Wilde behind. Hidalgo made his move before the second lap, and Hauser wasn’t able to respond. He quickly began to lose ground as the Brazilian looked comfortable all the way to the finish, taking the tape with an unmatched 14:20 5km.

It was a much-needed WTCS win to carry momentum into the 2027 Triathlon World Tour. Hauser shared afterward that he “could really feel the legs – and the whole year – in the back end of that race.”

Wilde crossed the line in third, comfortably ahead of the rest of the field, but a 14:52 5km left him short of the run speed he is accustomed to producing in these races. He won’t have much time to digest the result, however, as he immediately has to travel to Dubai, where he would look to continue his dominant T100 season.

#9012. How Beginners Can Build Cycling Endurance in Just 3 Days a Week

This coach-backed base training plan helps newer riders improve aerobic fitness, add structure, and make progress with limited time.

Building a base on the bike has traditionally meant putting in a lot of hours doing long, slow distance training. But with work and family lives, it can feel impossible to find the hours in the week to properly commit to a base build, especially if you’re a beginner cyclist who’s not used to rides that take more than three hours.

As it turns out, especially if you’re a newer cyclist, there’s a lot that you can accomplish if you only have three days a week to get on the bike. Building a base of fitness for cycling takes some commitment and consistency, but it doesn’t have to take over your life.

Here, we spoke with Namrita Brooke, Ph.D., one of the lead coaches at BaseCamp, about how she would structure the optimal three-day week on the bike—and what other lifestyle tweaks she would make in order to improve fitness even when you can’t fit in long rides.

A lot of cyclists think that if they can’t train 10-plus hours per week, their fitness will suffer, or they won’t make gains on the bike. This isn’t true, especially for newer riders. “Someone who has not been doing any exercise would see gains in as little as two to four hours a week of riding,” says Brooke. “If someone has some general fitness, gains could be had in four to six hours [per week].”

However, expect that after a few weeks or months, the tangible signs of progress will slow unless you can devote more time to training. “The tricky part is the ongoing gains might not be as easy to see as the initial gains,” Brooke adds. “Initially, if the athlete was measuring power, they would see power increases, but these would plateau in a few months, leading them to think gains are no longer occurring but in reality, the athlete is likely to still build other metrics of fitness like repeatability, durability, and resilience, but those are not as easy to measure.”

Often, new cyclists with limited time tend to attempt one monster ride on the weekend, skipping cycling during the week due to busy lives. But even if you can only eke out two one-hour (or 45-minute!) trainer sessions on weekdays in addition to the long weekend ride, you’ll gain fitness and strength faster than if you stick to a single ride.

“I would rather see the athlete do three quality days a week versus one or even two longer days,” says Brooke.

“The base training goal, whether you’re a pro or average Joe, is to build the best aerobic fitness you can for the training hours you have available,” says Brooke. Without this aerobic fitness, you won’t be able to boost your speed or power on the bike.

This means spending the bulk of your time on the bike in zone 2 (whether you use power, heart rate or perceived exertion). Riding in zone 2—also known as your endurance pace—will mean that you’re able to hold a conversation and speak in full sentences, but it should feel slightly difficult to do so. If you can chat away easily, you’re riding a little too easy. If you’re gasping for air between sentences, you’re riding a little too hard.

By that, we mean your skin. Riding more miles means being aware of skin considerations such as sun protection and chafing prevention. Don’t just ignore reddened skin, use lubricants and padded shorts to feel more comfortable on the bike.

For newer riders, opt for the longer durations in each phase. If you’ve been riding for a while, you’ll likely notice that after a few weeks in each phase, you’re at a point where you’re not noticing any improvements—in that case, proceed to the next phase. Here’s how Brooke would break it down.

2.5-3.5 hours (zone 2), based on how much free time you have available

New riders may need to break up the zone 3 portion of the ride with an easy 5-10 minutes in the middle.

2.5-4 hour (zone 2) based on how much free time you have available

Have an extra hour on Saturday for your long ride? Great! Woke up an hour early on Wednesday and have time to hop on the trainer for an extra 45-minute ride in zone 2? Fantastic. Feel free to add time whenever possible.

Four days on the bike is better than three, says Brooke. “Two harder interval days and two longer days would be best if possible,” she notes. And this is actually a fairly standard schedule for most serious cyclists—they’ll add one or two additional easy rides to the schedule, but the meat and potatoes of their training consists of two longer endurance rides and two harder interval-based sessions.

In fact, Brooke says that often, she hears new cyclists say they only have four hours per week to train, but once they get going, they start to “find” extra time. “You would be surprised how many newer riders think they are limited to four to six hours a week but once they really get into cycling, they make accommodations to squeeze in an extra hour or two per week,” she says. “I see riders all the time start to wake up earlier to squeeze in additional ride time before they start the rest of the day!”

And thanks to the prevalence of indoor trainers, it’s easier than ever to sneak in an extra hour or two on the bike during a weekend or early in the morning, even if you have work or childcare demands on your time. But don’t neglect outdoor riding, especially if your base-building goal is to be able to keep up on the local group ride or jump into a race. While indoor training builds fitness, it doesn’t help improve your skills for riding outdoors, so make time for at least one outdoor ride per week if at all possible.

There is one final caveat: It’s easy to get excited about the prospect of adding a monster ride to your weekend whenever possible, but these long rides aren’t easy. Four hours on the bike will feel very, very different from two hours. If riding for five hours on Saturday means you can barely walk for two days after, or it impacts your training the next week, back off.

Long rides shouldn’t leave you flattened for days afterwards. If they do, you’re doing too much, too soon. And Brooke notes that the longer you ride, the more important it is to properly fuel that long effort!

The fastest way to improve your fitness is—again—by consistently training. But training doesn’t mean all-bike-all-the-time! Brooke says there are quite a few simple additions you can do on those non-cycling days to see gains on the bike.

→ Walk: Often on conference calls for work, or accompanying your kiddos to soccer practice? Walk and talk, or do laps around the field while you cheer. “Walking is more of an aerobic builder than people think and can be a gentle form of aerobic activity to accompany bike time,” Brooke says.

For the office worker, treadmill desks are becoming more popular, and if you do want to put in more bike time and you have a stationary trainer, you can do some easy spinning while answering emails or brainstorming for that big presentation.

→ Strength Train: “Strength training can be added in as little as 15 minutes a day, three days a week if we are willing to change the paradigm of going to the gym and lifting heavy things,” says Brooke. “Integrating just this small amount of functional strength into a base training program like we do at BaseCamp yields long-term benefits to your training and health.”

You can do shortstrength sessions at home with just a couple of weights, or even bodyweight alone to get started.

In a typical training plan, cyclists have three weeks of training followed by a rest week where they do only a couple of shorter, easier rides. When you’re only able to ride three days a week, there’s no reason to take a rest week—you’re already getting plenty of recovery time in the four days you’re off the bike.

“The low training stimulus is likely not enough to elicit a high enough super-compensation response to make the loss of fitness during a rest week worth it,” says Brooke. (That said, if you’re a beginner rider and find that after three weeks, you are feeling fatigued, you can dial down the duration or intensity for that fourth week—but stick to three rides if possible.)

Once you’ve done your base training for several weeks with your rides spread out through the week (i.e Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday), you may want to try switching things up. If you do have the ability to try out new riding days, it’s worth experimenting with doing mini-training blocks, i.e riding three days in a row, some weeks. This subtle shift changes your training stimulus by forcing your body to contend with the need for speedier recovery between rides.

Newer riders may find that it’s harder to recover between rides in these chunks, says Brooke. “The challenge of block training is the athlete needs a certain amount of base fitness to be able to respond and adapt to this type of stimuli and in this scenario,” she explains. “But testing the block process is the only way to find out how they tolerate it.”

If you try riding three days in a row and feel exhausted, go back to your regular schedule and test again after another few weeks of consistent training.

While it’s tempting to stay in the base phase forever, this training phase should really only last around eight weeks. At this point, your aerobic fitness is maximized (for now) and it’s time to focus on the development of “power.”

“After the base phase comes the build phase, where the athlete wants to increase their sustainable max power for a range of times,” says Brooke. “For a newer cyclist without a specific goal, focus on holding a higher wattage for five minutes to 40 minutes. This phase should be maintained as long as the athlete continues to see improvement, then once response begins to fade, move on to the next phases.”

Once you’ve plateaued your power gains, the final phase, typically utilized when “peaking” for an event would be the “speed” phase, explains Brooke. “Here, the cyclist would focus on improving shorter efforts of under five minutes and building anaerobic capacity to focus on performing better in events or group rides.”

After your main event, whether it’s a race or group ride or even just spending four to six weeks focusing on upping your sprint power, it’s time to take a short break and then circle back to base phase.

The good news is that once you’ve completed this cycle, you’ll be pleasantly surprised at how much stronger you’re feeling on the bike the second time you tackle base training. While training phases are cyclical, your fitness grows as you spend more and more time on the bike, so no training phase will feel exactly the same.

A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that currently average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most important financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.
